1. Introduction to Operating Systems

What is an Operating System?

An Operating System is system software that acts as an interface between the user or application programs and the computer hardware. It manages and allocates system resources such as CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices among different programs. It also provides a platform or environment in which application programs can run efficiently and securely.

Examples of Operating Systems

  • Windows (Microsoft)
  • Ubuntu (Linux distribution)
  • Debian (Linux distribution)
  • Fedora (Linux distribution)
  • macOS (Apple)
  • Android (Google)
  • iOS (Apple)
  • ChromeOS (Google)
  • Tizen (Samsung)
  • Unix (Multi-user operating system)

Is Linux an Operating System?

Linux technically refers to the kernel. Operating systems such as Ubuntu and Debian use the Linux kernel along with other system software. So Ubuntu is a Linux distribution, while Linux itself is the kernel.

Goals of Operating System

Primary Goals:

  • Convenience: Make the computer easy and convenient for users.
  • Efficiency: Utilize hardware resources efficiently.

Secondary Goals:

  • Security: Protect data and system resources.
  • Reliability: Ensure stable and error-free operation.
  • Scalability: Support increasing users, processes, and resources.
  • Maintainability: Make the system easy to update and manage.

Functions of Operating System

  1. Process Management: Creates, schedules, and terminates processes.
  2. Memory Management: Allocates and deallocates memory to processes.
  3. I/O Management: Manages input/output devices like keyboard, disk, and printer.
  4. File Management: Creates, organizes, stores, and manages files and permissions.
  5. Network Management: Manages network connections and data communication.
  6. Security & Protection: Protects the system through authentication and access control.

Types of Operating Systems

1. Batch Operating System

“A Batch OS executes a group of jobs in batches without user interaction. Jobs with similar requirements are grouped together and executed sequentially.”

Example: Payroll processing, bank statement generation.

Key point: No direct user interaction.

2. Multiprogramming Operating System

“A multiprogramming OS keeps multiple programs in memory at the same time and switches the CPU to another program when one is waiting for I/O, improving CPU utilization.”

Key point: Multiple programs in memory → better CPU utilization.

3. Multitasking Operating System

“A multitasking OS allows multiple tasks or applications to appear to run simultaneously by rapidly switching the CPU between them.”

Example: Listening to music while browsing and downloading a file.

Key point: Multiple tasks at the same time.

4. Time-Sharing Operating System

Time-Sharing is a specific form of multitasking that supports multiple users on the same computer system.

“A time-sharing OS gives each process or user a small time slice of CPU time, allowing multiple users or processes to interact with the system simultaneously.”

Key point: CPU time is divided into time slices.

5. Multiprocessing Operating System

“A multiprocessing OS uses two or more CPUs or processor cores to execute processes in parallel, improving performance and reliability.”

Key point: Multiple processors → parallel execution.

6. Distributed Operating System

“A distributed OS manages multiple connected computers and makes them appear to users as a single unified system.”

Key point: Multiple computers → single system view.

7. Network Operating System

“A Network OS is designed to manage and provide services over a network, such as file sharing, printer sharing, and user management.”

Examples: Windows Server, Linux server distributions.

Key point: Provides network-based services.

8. Real-Time Operating System (RTOS)

“A real-time OS guarantees that tasks are completed within a specified time constraint. It is commonly used where timing is critical.”

Hard Real-Time

“Missing a deadline is unacceptable and can cause system failure.”

Examples: Aircraft control systems, medical critical systems.

Soft Real-Time

“Missing an occasional deadline is acceptable, but it may reduce system performance.”

Examples: Video streaming, online gaming.

Key point: Hard = deadline must be met; Soft = occasional delay is acceptable.

9. Mobile Operating System

“A Mobile OS is designed specifically for smartphones and tablets, providing features such as touch interaction, mobile networking, power management, and app management.”

Examples: Android, iOS.

Key point: Designed for mobile devices.

Easy Way to Remember

  • Multiprogramming → Keep multiple programs in memory.
  • Multitasking → Run multiple tasks seemingly simultaneously.
  • Time-sharing → Share CPU time fairly using time slices.
  • Multiprocessing → Use multiple CPUs/cores for parallel execution.

Importance of Operating System

  • Manages Resources: CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices.
  • Runs Applications: Provides an environment for programs to execute.
  • Provides Security: Protects data and system resources.
  • User Interface: Provides CLI/GUI for user interaction.
  • Ensures Efficiency: Improves resource utilization and system performance.
  • Handles Errors: Detects and manages system errors.

OS Interface

Interview-ready answer:

“An OS interface is the way through which a user or application interacts with the operating system to perform tasks.”

Types of OS Interface

InterfaceDescriptionExample
CLIUser interacts using commandsLinux Terminal, Command Prompt
GUIUser interacts using windows, icons, menus, etc.Windows, macOS
System Call InterfaceApplications interact with OS services through system callsopen(), read(), write()

Easy to Remember

User → Interface → OS → Hardware

2. Operating System Architecture & The Kernel

What is Kernel?

The kernel is the core component of an operating system. It acts as a bridge between applications and hardware and manages important resources such as CPU, memory, processes, and I/O devices.

Is the Kernel the Same as the Operating System?

“No. The kernel is the core part of the operating system, while an operating system also includes other components such as system utilities, libraries, drivers, and user interfaces.”

User Mode and Kernel Mode

Modern operating systems use two execution modes to protect the system:

1. User Mode

  • Used by normal applications like Chrome, VS Code, etc.
  • Has limited access to hardware and system resources.
  • Cannot directly execute privileged instructions.
  • If an application needs OS services, it uses a system call.

2. Kernel Mode

  • Used by the OS kernel.
  • Has full access to hardware and system resources.
  • Can execute privileged instructions.
  • Handles tasks like memory management, process scheduling, and device management.

Mode Bit

“A mode bit is a hardware flag used by the CPU to indicate whether the current process is running in user mode or kernel mode.”

Typically:

  • Mode bit = 1 → User Mode
  • Mode bit = 0 → Kernel Mode

Does Kernel Run All the Time?

“The kernel is always present in memory while the operating system is running, but it does not continuously execute. The CPU runs kernel code when it needs to perform OS-related tasks, such as handling system calls, interrupts, process scheduling, or hardware operations. Otherwise, the CPU can execute user-level programs.”

Functions of Kernel

  • Process Management: Creates, schedules, and terminates processes.
  • Memory Management: Allocates and manages memory.
  • Device Management: Controls hardware devices.
  • File Management: Handles file and storage operations.
  • Inter-Process Communication (IPC): Enables processes to communicate and share data.
  • System Calls: Provides OS services to applications.
  • Security & Protection: Controls access to system resources.

Types of Kernel

There are mainly 5 types of kernels:

1. Monolithic Kernel

  • All major OS services run in kernel space.
  • Fast but less isolated.
  • Example: Linux, Unix.

2. Microkernel

  • Only essential services run in kernel space.
  • Other services run in user space.
  • More secure and modular but may have performance overhead.
  • Example: MINIX, QNX.

3. Hybrid Kernel

  • Combines features of monolithic and microkernel designs.
  • Example: Windows NT, macOS (XNU).

4. Exokernel

  • Provides very low-level hardware access to applications.
  • Gives applications more control over resources.
  • Example: MIT Exokernel.

5. Nano Kernel

  • Provides an extremely small set of basic hardware-level functions.
  • Focuses on minimalism and efficiency.

What is an Interrupt?

An interrupt is a signal sent to the CPU/Kernal by hardware or software to indicate that an event needs immediate attention. The CPU temporarily pauses its current execution, handles the interrupt through the operating system, and then resumes the previous task.

Types of Interrupts

Hardware Interrupt

  • Generated by hardware devices.
  • Example: Keyboard input, mouse click, network packet.

Software Interrupt

  • Generated by software/programs.
  • Example: System calls or software-generated exceptions.

How an Interrupt Works

Event → Interrupt → CPU pauses current task → Kernel handles it → CPU resumes task

What is a System Call?

“A system call is a mechanism through which a user-level application requests a service from the operating system kernel. Since applications cannot directly access privileged resources, they use system calls to request services such as file operations, process creation, memory management, and device access.”

Why are System Calls Needed?

Applications run in user mode, while sensitive OS operations require kernel mode.

Common Types of System Calls

  • Process Management: fork(), exec(), exit()
  • File Management: open(), read(), write(), close()
  • Memory Management: mmap(), brk()
  • Device Management: Device read/write operations
  • Interprocess Communication: Pipes, shared memory, sockets
  • Protection: Access control and permissions

How Do System Calls Work?

“A system call provides a controlled way for a user program to request a service from the OS kernel.”

Steps:

  1. System Call: Program requests an OS service.
  2. Mode Switch: CPU switches from User Mode → Kernel Mode.
  3. Identify Call: Kernel identifies the system call using its system call number.
  4. Execute: Kernel performs the requested operation.
  5. Return Result: Kernel returns the result to the program.
  6. Mode Switch: CPU switches back from Kernel Mode → User Mode.

System Call Flow

User Program → System Call → Kernel Mode → Kernel executes → Result → User Mode

What Happens When We Turn On a Computer?

When we turn on a computer, the system goes through a booting process. First, the hardware is powered on and the firmware performs a hardware check. Then the bootloader is loaded, which loads the operating system kernel into memory. The kernel initializes hardware, memory, processes, and other OS components. Finally, the system starts the login screen or desktop environment.

Steps

  1. Power On – CPU starts executing firmware instructions.
  2. POST – BIOS/UEFI checks essential hardware.
  3. Bootloader Loads – Firmware finds and loads the bootloader.
  4. Kernel Loads – Bootloader loads the OS kernel into RAM.
  5. Kernel Initialization – Kernel initializes CPU, memory, devices, drivers, etc.
  6. System Services Start – Required OS services and background processes start.
  7. Login/Desktop – User gets the login screen or desktop.

Easy Flow

Power ON → BIOS/UEFI → POST → Bootloader → Kernel → OS Services → Login/Desktop

BIOS Full Form

BIOS = Basic Input/Output System

It is firmware stored on the motherboard that initializes hardware and starts the booting process.

Structure of Operating System

OS structure defines how the components of an operating system are organized and interact with each other.

1. Simple Structure

  • No well-defined structure between OS components.
  • Components can directly interact with each other.
  • Example: Early MS-DOS.
  • Advantage: Simple and fast.
  • Disadvantage: Difficult to maintain and secure.

2. Monolithic Structure

  • All major OS services run in kernel space.
  • Components can directly communicate with each other.
  • Example: Linux, Unix.
  • Advantage: High performance.
  • Disadvantage: A bug in one component can affect the entire kernel.

3. Layered Structure

  • OS is divided into multiple layers.
  • Each layer uses services provided by the layer below it.
  • Advantage: Easy to design, debug, and maintain.
  • Disadvantage: Can introduce performance overhead.

4. Microkernel Structure

  • Only essential services run in the kernel.
  • Other services such as drivers and file systems run in user space.
  • Example: MINIX, QNX.
  • Advantage: Better security and reliability.
  • Disadvantage: Communication between components can add overhead.

5. Modular Structure

  • Kernel is divided into modules.
  • Modules can be dynamically loaded or removed when needed.
  • Example: Linux supports loadable kernel modules.
  • Advantage: Flexible and easier to extend.

6. Hybrid Structure

  • Combines features of monolithic and microkernel approaches.
  • Provides performance while maintaining some modularity.
  • Examples: Windows NT, macOS XNU.

7. Solaris Structure

  • Oracle Solaris uses a modular architecture with a core kernel and dynamically loadable modules.
  • It combines features such as monolithic kernel performance and modular design.

Quick Interview Revision

Simple → Monolithic → Layered → Microkernel → Modular → Hybrid → Solaris

The most important comparison to remember:

Monolithic = everything in kernel space Microkernel = minimum in kernel space Layered = organized into layers Modular = components can be dynamically added/removed Hybrid = combination of approaches

3. Process Management & Inter-Process Communication

What is a Process?

“A process is a program that is currently in execution. It is an active entity that has its own memory, CPU state, resources, and execution context.”

Program vs Process

  • Program: Passive set of instructions stored on disk.
  • Process: Active instance of a program running in memory.

“A program is a passive entity containing a set of instructions stored on secondary storage, such as an executable file. It becomes a process when the executable is loaded into main memory and the operating system creates its PCB. A process is an active entity that requires resources such as CPU time, memory, and registers for execution.

Key Points

  • Program → Passive entity
    • Stored on secondary storage.
    • Contains instructions.
    • Does not require CPU or memory for execution.
  • Process → Active entity
    • Program loaded into main memory.
    • Has a PCB (Process Control Block).
    • Requires CPU, memory, registers, and other resources.
  • Same Program ≠ Same Process
    • Multiple instances of the same program can create separate processes.
    • They have separate execution states and memory such as stack, heap, and data.

Example:

“If I open multiple instances of a browser, each running instance can be represented as a separate process, even though they may share the same program code.”

AspectProgramProcess
Nature / DefinitionPassive entity; static set of instructionsActive entity; execution of a program
StateStored on disk; no active execution stateDynamic states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated
ExistenceExists as a file on diskExists temporarily during execution
MemoryTakes storage space on diskUses RAM, CPU, registers, etc.
IdentifierNo unique identifier requiredHas a unique PID (Process ID)

Memory Layout of a Process

“The memory layout of a process describes how a process is organized in main memory during execution.”

A process is typically divided into these sections:

1. Text / Code

  • Contains the program's executable instructions.
  • Usually read-only.

2. Data

  • Contains global and static variables.
  • Divided into initialized and uninitialized data.

3. Heap

  • Used for dynamic memory allocation.
  • Grows/shrinks during execution.
  • Example: new, malloc().

4. Stack

  • Stores function calls, local variables, parameters, and return addresses.
  • Automatically managed during function execution.

Attributes of a Process

The attributes of a process are the information the OS maintains to manage and control a process.

These attributes are stored in a structure called the Process Control Block (PCB) (sometimes called a task control block).

  • Process ID (PID): Unique identifier of the process.
  • Process State: Current state such as New, Ready, Running, Waiting, or Terminated.
  • Program Counter: Address of the next instruction to execute.
  • CPU Registers: Stores the current CPU state of the process.
  • CPU Scheduling Information: Priority and scheduling-related information.
  • Memory Information: Details about the memory allocated to the process.
  • I/O Information: Information about files and I/O devices used by the process.
  • Accounting Information: CPU usage, execution time, and other resource usage.

Does a Running Process Access Its PCB from Main Memory?

“The PCB is maintained and managed by the operating system in kernel memory. A process does not directly access its own PCB. The kernel accesses and updates the PCB whenever it needs to manage the process.

Process Control Block (PCB)

“A Process Control Block, or PCB, is a data structure maintained by the operating system that stores all important information about a process. The OS uses the PCB to manage, schedule, and track the process.

What does PCB contain?

  • Process ID (PID): Unique identifier of the process.
  • Process State: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, or Terminated.
  • Program Counter: Address of the next instruction to execute.
  • CPU Registers: Stores the CPU state of the process.
  • Scheduling Information: Priority, scheduling queue information, etc.
  • Memory Management Information: Memory allocated to the process.
  • I/O Information: Files and I/O devices used by the process.
  • Accounting Information: CPU time and other resource usage.

Why is PCB important?

“PCB allows the OS to stop, resume, and manage processes. It is especially important during context switching, because the OS saves the state of one process in its PCB and restores the state of another process from its PCB.”

Process Table

“A Process Table is a data structure maintained by the operating system that contains information about all the active processes in the system. Each entry in the process table typically points to or contains the PCB of a process

Key Points

  • Contains one entry for each process.
  • Stores or references the process's PCB.
  • Helps the OS track and manage processes.
  • Used during process scheduling, context switching, and resource management.

Process Management

“Process management is an operating system function responsible for creating, scheduling, executing, synchronizing, and terminating processes. It ensures that processes get the required CPU and other resources efficiently

Main Functions of process management

  • Process Creation: Creates new processes.
  • Process Scheduling: Decides which process gets the CPU.
  • Context Switching: Switches CPU between processes.
  • Process Synchronization: Coordinates processes sharing resources.
  • IPC: Enables processes to communicate and exchange data.
  • Resource Allocation: Allocates CPU, memory, and I/O resources.
  • Process Termination: Terminates completed or failed processes.
  • Deadlock Handling: Detects, prevents, avoids, or recovers from deadlocks.

Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

“Inter-Process Communication, or IPC, is a mechanism provided by the operating system that allows processes to communicate and exchange data with each other.

Why is IPC Needed?

Processes normally have separate memory spaces, so one process cannot directly access another process's memory. IPC provides controlled ways for them to share data and coordinate their execution.

Main IPC Methods

  1. Shared Memory
    • Processes share a common memory region.
    • Very fast because data doesn't need to be repeatedly copied.
    • Requires synchronization to avoid race conditions.
  1. Message Passing
    • Processes communicate by sending and receiving messages.
    • Safer and easier to manage than shared memory.
    • Can be implemented using pipes, message queues, sockets, etc.

IPC Mechanisms

The main IPC mechanisms are:

  1. Pipes
    • Used for communication between processes.
    • Commonly used between related processes.
    • Example: ls | grep txt
  2. Named Pipes (FIFO)
    • Similar to pipes but can be used by unrelated processes.
  3. Message Queues
    • Processes communicate by sending and receiving messages through a queue.
  4. Shared Memory
    • Multiple processes share a memory region.
    • Fastest IPC mechanism, but requires synchronization.
  5. Semaphores
    • Used mainly for process synchronization and controlling access to shared resources.
    • Not primarily used to transfer data.
  6. Sockets
    • Allow processes to communicate locally or over a network.
    • Common in client-server applications.
  7. Signals
    • Used to notify a process that a particular event has occurred.
    • Example: SIGKILL, SIGINT.

Context Switching

“Context switching is the process of saving the state of a currently running process and loading the saved state of another process, so the CPU can switch between them.”

How it works

  1. Current process is running.
  2. An interrupt, system call, or scheduler decision occurs.
  3. OS saves the current process's CPU state in its PCB.
  4. OS selects another process.
  5. OS loads the new process's saved state from its PCB.
  6. CPU resumes execution of the new process.

What is saved?

The context can include:

  • Program Counter
  • CPU Registers
  • Process State
  • Other CPU execution information

Process States

A process state represents the current status of a process during its lifecycle.

The 5 basic process states are:

  1. New
    • Process is being created.
  2. Ready
    • Process is ready to run but waiting for CPU allocation.
  3. Running
    • Process is currently executing on the CPU.
  4. Waiting / Blocked
    • Process is waiting for an event, usually I/O completion.
  5. Terminated
    • Process has finished execution or has been terminated.

Seven-State Process Model

The seven-state process model extends the basic five-state model by adding two suspended states. These states are useful when a process is temporarily moved from main memory to secondary storage.

7 Process States

  1. New
    • Process is being created.
  2. Ready
    • Process is in memory and waiting for CPU.
  3. Running
    • Process is currently executing.
  4. Blocked / Waiting
    • Process is waiting for an event or I/O.
  5. Terminated
    • Process has completed or been terminated.
  6. Ready Suspended
    • Process is ready to execute but has been moved from main memory to secondary storage.
  7. Blocked Suspended
    • Process is waiting for an event and has been moved from main memory to secondary storage.

Important Transitions

  • Ready → Ready Suspended: Process is swapped out of memory.
  • Ready Suspended → Ready: Process is brought back into memory.
  • Blocked → Blocked Suspended: Blocked process is swapped out.
  • Blocked Suspended → Blocked: Process is brought back while still waiting.
  • Blocked Suspended → Ready Suspended: The event it was waiting for occurs while it is suspended.

CPU-Bound Process (CPU-Intensive)

“A CPU-bound process spends most of its time performing CPU computations and requires very little I/O.”

  • Requires more CPU time.
  • Performs heavy calculations.
  • I/O operations are relatively less frequent.
  • Example: Video encoding, mathematical calculations, scientific simulations.

I/O-Bound Process (I/O-Intensive)

“An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O operations and requires relatively less CPU computation.”

  • Requires more I/O operations.
  • Frequently waits for disk, network, keyboard, etc.
  • CPU bursts are usually shorter.
  • Example: File copying, database queries, web server requests.

Easy way to remember:

CPU-Bound → More CPU work, less waiting I/O-Bound → More I/O waiting, less CPU work

Types of Processes

Processes can be classified based on their behavior, relationship, and purpose.

  1. CPU-Bound Process
    • Spends most of its time using the CPU.
    • Example: Video encoding, complex calculations.
  2. I/O-Bound Process
    • Spends most of its time waiting for I/O.
    • Example: File or network operations.
  3. Parent Process
    • A process that creates another process.
    • The newly created process is called its child.
  4. Child Process
    • A process created by another process (parent).
  5. Independent Process
    • Does not affect or depend on other processes.
    • Does not share data/state with other processes.
  6. Cooperating Process
    • Can affect or be affected by other processes.
    • Communicates using IPC and may share data.
  7. Zombie Process
    • A process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet collected its exit status.
  8. Orphan Process
    • A process whose parent has terminated while the child is still running.
    • It is adopted by another system process.
  9. Daemon Process
    • A background process that provides services without direct user interaction.
    • Example: Web server, logging service.

10. Swapper Process

  • A system process responsible for swapping processes between main memory and secondary storage.
  • Helps manage memory under certain OS designs.

Important Interview Differences

Zombie vs Orphan:

Zombie → Child has finished, parent hasn't collected its status. Orphan → Parent has finished, child is still running.

Independent vs Cooperating:

Independent → Doesn't interact with other processes. Cooperating → Communicates/interacts with other processes.

Schedulers

Schedulers are components of an operating system that decide which process should be executed by the CPU at a given time.

Schedulers

“A scheduler is an OS component that decides which processes should be admitted to the system, kept in memory, or given the CPU.”

There are three main types of schedulers:

1. Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler)

  • Selects processes from the job pool waiting on the disk(secondary storage) and loads them into main memory(ready queue).
  • Controls the degree of multiprogramming.
  • Runs relatively infrequently.

2. Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler)

  • Selects a process from the Ready Queue and assigns the CPU.
  • Short-term scheduler will decide which process is to be executed next and then it will call the dispatcher. A dispatcher is a software that moves the process from ready to run and vice versa. In other words, it is context switching.
  • Runs very frequently, so it must be fast.

3. Medium-Term Scheduler

  • Temporarily removes processes from memory (swap out) and later brings them back (swap in).
  • Helps manage memory and degree of multiprogramming.
  • The swapping is done to reduce degree of multiprogramming

Easy Interview Trick

Long-Term → Selects jobs Medium-Term → Swaps processes Short-Term → Selects CPU process

Flow:

Job Pool → Long-Term Scheduler → Ready Queue → Short-Term Scheduler → CPU

Medium-Term Scheduler: can move processes Memory ↔ Secondary Storage.

Scheduling Queues

“Scheduling queues are queues maintained by the operating system to keep track of processes waiting for different resources.”

1. Job Queue

  • Contains all processes in the system.
  • Managed mainly by the Long-Term Scheduler.
  • Processes wait here before being admitted to memory.

2. Ready Queue

  • Contains processes that are in main memory and ready to execute.
  • They wait for CPU allocation.
  • Managed by the Short-Term Scheduler.

3. Device / Waiting Queue

  • Contains processes waiting for an I/O device or event.
  • Example: A process waiting for disk I/O.

Dispatcher

“The dispatcher is an OS component that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.”

In other words, the dispatcher is the module that performs the actual context switching and process execution.

Main Functions

  1. Context Switching: Saves the current process state and loads the selected process state.
  2. Switch to User Mode: Changes CPU from kernel mode to user mode when required.
  3. Jump to Correct Location: Transfers control to the selected process's next instruction.

Scheduler vs Dispatcher

  • Scheduler: Decides which process should run.
  • Dispatcher: Actually gives the CPU to that process.

Dispatch Latency

“Dispatch latency is the time taken by the dispatcher to stop one process and start executing another process.”

It includes the time taken for:

o Saving the state of the current process.

o Loading the state of the new process.

o Performing context switching.

Context Switching

“Context switching is the process in which the OS saves the state of the currently running process and restores the state of another process, allowing the CPU to switch between processes.”

Steps

  1. Save Current Process
    • OS saves the CPU state, such as registers and Program Counter, into the process's PCB.
  2. Select Next Process
    • Short-Term Scheduler selects a process from the Ready Queue.
  3. Restore Next Process
    • OS loads the selected process's saved state from its PCB.
  4. Resume Execution
    • CPU starts executing the selected process from where it was previously stopped.

Degree of Multiprogramming The number of processes that can reside in the ready state at maximum decides the degree of multiprogramming, e.g., if the degree of programming = 100, this means 100 processes can reside in the ready state at maximum.

4. CPU Scheduling & Dispatching

CPU Scheduling

“CPU scheduling is the process by which the operating system selects one process from the ready queue and allocates the CPU to it. The main goal is to use the CPU efficiently and provide good system performance and response time.”

Why is CPU Scheduling Needed?

  • Multiple processes may be ready at the same time.
  • Usually, only one process can use a CPU core at a time.
  • The OS needs to decide which process should run next.

Who Performs It?

  • Short-Term Scheduler: Selects the next process.
  • Dispatcher: Gives the CPU to the selected process.

Types of CPU Scheduling

CPU scheduling is mainly divided into Preemptive and Non-Preemptive scheduling.

1. Non-Preemptive Scheduling

  • Once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it finishes or enters the waiting state (e.g., by waiting for I/O) .
  • OS cannot forcibly take the CPU away.
  • Examples: FCFS, SJF, Non-Preemptive Priority.

2. Preemptive Scheduling

  • OS can forcibly take the CPU from a running process and assign it to another process.
  • Useful for multitasking and interactive systems.
  • Examples: Round Robin, SRTF, Preemptive Priority.

Easy Interview Difference

Non-Preemptive → Process gives up CPU voluntarily. Preemptive → OS can take CPU away from the process.

Starvation

“Starvation is a situation where a process waits for an indefinitely long time because other processes keep getting the required resources or CPU before it.”

Example:

In Priority Scheduling, if high-priority processes continuously arrive, a low-priority process may keep waiting and never get CPU time.

Cause

  • Continuous arrival of higher-priority processes.
  • Unfair resource allocation.
  • Poor scheduling policy.

Solution

Aging is the common solution.

“Aging gradually increases the priority of a waiting process so that it eventually gets CPU time.”

Scheduling Criteria

Scheduling criteria are the parameters used to evaluate and compare CPU scheduling algorithms.

  1. CPU Utilization
    • Keep the CPU as busy as possible.
    • Goal: Maximize
  2. Throughput
    • Number of processes completed per unit time.
    • Goal: Maximize
  3. Turnaround Time
    • Total time taken from arrival to completion.
    • Goal: Minimize
  4. Waiting Time
    • Total time a process waits in the ready queue.
    • Goal: Minimize
  5. Response Time
    • Time from request submission until the first response.
    • Goal: Minimize
  6. Fairness
    • Ensure every process gets a reasonable chance to execute.
    • Goal: Avoid starvation

Interview shortcut:

Maximize: CPU Utilization, Throughput Minimize: Turnaround Time, Waiting Time, Response Time Ensure: Fairness

Note: The CPU-scheduling algorithm does not affect the amount of time during which a process executes or perform I/0; it affects only the amount of time that a process spends waiting in the ready queue.

Goodput refer to the number of processes completed per unit time.

Terminologies Used in CPU Scheduling

  1. Arrival Time (AT)
    • Time at which a process enters the Ready Queue.
  2. Burst Time (BT)
    • Total CPU time required by a process for execution.
  3. Completion Time (CT)
    • Time at which a process finishes execution.
  4. Turnaround Time (TAT)
    • Total time taken from arrival to completion.
    • TAT = CT − AT
  5. Waiting Time (WT)
    • Total time a process waits in the Ready Queue.
    • WT = TAT − BT
  6. Response Time (RT)
    • Time from arrival until the process gets CPU for the first time.
    • RT = First CPU Start Time − AT
  7. CPU Burst
    • Continuous period during which a process uses the CPU.
  8. I/O Burst
    • Period during which a process performs or waits for I/O operations.
  9. Time Quantum
    • Fixed CPU time allocated to a process in Round Robin scheduling.

10. Context Switch

  • Switching the CPU from one process to another.

Most Important Formulas

TAT = CT − AT WT = TAT − BT RT = First Start Time − AT

CPU Scheduling Algorithms

CPU scheduling algorithms decide which process from the Ready Queue gets the CPU next.

AlgorithmTypeBasic Idea
FCFSNon-PreemptiveProcess that arrives first gets CPU first
SJFNon-PreemptiveProcess with the shortest burst time runs first
SRTFPreemptiveProcess with the shortest remaining time runs first
LJFNon-PreemptiveProcess with the longest burst time runs first
LRTFPreemptiveProcess with the longest remaining time runs first
Priority SchedulingNon-PreemptiveHighest-priority process runs first
Priority SchedulingPreemptiveHigher-priority process can preempt the current process
Round RobinPreemptiveEach process gets a fixed time quantum in cyclic order
HRRNNon-PreemptiveProcess with the highest response ratio runs first
Multilevel QueueUsually PreemptiveReady queue is divided into multiple separate queues
Multilevel Feedback QueuePreemptiveProcesses can move between queues based on their behavior

Important Formulas

HRRN:

Response Ratio = (Waiting Time + Burst Time) / Burst Time

Easy Interview Revision

  • FCFS → First come, first served
  • SJF → Shortest burst
  • SRTF → Shortest remaining time
  • LJF → Longest burst
  • LRTF → Longest remaining time
  • Priority → Highest priority
  • Round Robin → Fixed time quantum
  • HRRN → Highest response ratio
  • MLQ → Separate fixed queues
  • MLFQ → Processes can move between queues

FCFS (First Come First Serve)

“FCFS is a non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm in which the process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first. Once a process gets the CPU, it runs until it finishes or enters a waiting state.”

How It Works

  • Processes are executed according to their Arrival Time.
  • It follows the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle.
  • It is non-preemptive.
  • Once CPU is allocated, another process cannot forcibly take it.

Convoy Effect

“Convoy effect occurs when a long CPU-bound process holds the CPU for a long time, causing many short processes to wait behind it.”

it results into more average waiting time.

Solution, smaller process has to be executed before longer process, to achieve less average waiting time.

Advantages

  • Simple and easy to implement.
  • Fair based on arrival order.
  • No starvation.

Disadvantages

  • Can cause Convoy Effect.
  • Average waiting time can be high.
  • Poor response time for interactive systems.

SJF (Shortest Job First)

“SJF is a non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm in which the process with the shortest CPU burst time is selected first. Once a process starts executing, it continues until it finishes or enters a waiting state.”

How It Works

  • Selects the process with the smallest burst time.
  • It is non-preemptive.
  • If multiple processes have the same burst time, FCFS can be used as a tie-breaker.
  • It generally provides the minimum average waiting time when burst times are known accurately.

Advantages

  • Minimum average waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms under ideal conditions.
  • Better average turnaround time than FCFS in many cases.

Disadvantages

  • Can cause starvation for long processes.
  • CPU burst time must be known or estimated.
  • Not ideal for interactive systems.

Why does SJF give minimum average waiting time?

“Because executing shorter jobs first reduces the amount of time that subsequent processes have to wait.”

SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First)

“SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF. It always selects the process with the shortest remaining CPU burst time. If a new process arrives with a shorter remaining time than the currently running process, the current process is preempted.”

How It Works

  • It is preemptive.
  • The scheduler continuously considers the remaining burst time.
  • A newly arrived process can preempt the currently running process.
  • If two processes have the same remaining time, FCFS can be used as a tie-breaker.

Advantages

  • Usually gives low average waiting time.
  • Provides good response for short processes.
  • Better than SJF when processes arrive at different times.

Disadvantages

  • Can cause starvation for long processes.
  • More context switching due to preemption.
  • Requires knowledge/estimation of remaining CPU burst time.

SJF vs SRTF

SJF → Non-preemptive → Shortest burst time SRTF → Preemptive → Shortest remaining time

LJF (Longest Job First)

“LJF is a non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm in which the process with the longest CPU burst time is selected first. Once the process gets the CPU, it continues until completion or until it enters a waiting state.”

How It Works

  • Selects the process with the largest burst time.
  • Non-preemptive scheduling.
  • If two processes have the same burst time, FCFS can be used as a tie-breaker.

Advantages

  • Simple to implement.
  • Long CPU-intensive processes get priority.

Disadvantages

  • Short processes may suffer long waiting times.
  • Can cause starvation of short processes.
  • Generally poor average waiting and response time.

LRTF (Longest Remaining Time First)

“LRTF is the preemptive version of LJF. It always selects the process with the longest remaining CPU burst time. If a new process has a longer remaining time than the currently running process, the current process is preempted.”

How It Works

  • Preemptive scheduling algorithm.
  • Selects the process with the longest remaining burst time.
  • A newly arrived process can preempt the running process.
  • Scheduling decisions are made whenever a process arrives or the remaining times change.

Advantages

  • Gives preference to long CPU-intensive processes.
  • Can be useful when long jobs should receive CPU priority.

Disadvantages

  • Short processes can suffer starvation.
  • Frequent preemption can cause high context-switching overhead.
  • Generally poor response time for short/interactive processes.

LJF vs LRTF

LJF → Non-preemptive → Longest burst time LRTF → Preemptive → Longest remaining time

Priority Scheduling (Non-Preemptive)

“In non-preemptive priority scheduling, the process with the highest priority is selected from the ready queue and given the CPU. Once it starts executing, it continues until it finishes or enters a waiting state.”

How It Works

  • Each process is assigned a priority.
  • The process with the highest priority runs first.
  • It is non-preemptive, so a running process cannot be forcibly interrupted by a newly arrived higher-priority process.
  • If two processes have the same priority, FCFS can be used as a tie-breaker.

Advantages

  • Simple and flexible.
  • Important/high-priority processes get CPU first.
  • Useful when processes have different levels of importance.

Disadvantages

  • Low-priority processes may suffer starvation.
  • Priority assignment can be difficult.
  • Poor priority design can lead to unfair CPU allocation.

Solution to Starvation

Aging:

“Aging gradually increases the priority of a waiting process so that it eventually gets CPU time.”

Priority Scheduling (Preemptive)

“In preemptive priority scheduling, the process with the highest priority gets the CPU. If a new process arrives with a higher priority than the currently running process, the current process is preempted and the new process gets the CPU.”

How It Works

  • Each process has a priority.
  • The highest-priority process is selected.
  • It is preemptive.
  • A newly arrived higher-priority process can interrupt the running process.
  • If priorities are equal, FCFS can be used as a tie-breaker.

Advantages

  • High-priority processes get quick CPU access.
  • Good for systems where some tasks are more important than others.
  • Provides better response for high-priority processes.

Disadvantages

  • Can cause starvation of low-priority processes.
  • More context switching.
  • Priority assignment must be carefully designed.

Solution to Starvation

Aging:

“Aging gradually increases the priority of processes that have been waiting for a long time.”

Non-Preemptive vs Preemptive Priority

Non-Preemptive → Running process keeps CPU. Preemptive → Higher-priority process can take CPU from running process.

Round Robin (RR)

Interview-ready answer:

“Round Robin is a preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm designed mainly for time-sharing systems. Each process gets a fixed amount of CPU time called a time quantum. After its time quantum expires, the process is preempted and moved to the end of the ready queue.”

How It Works

  1. Processes are placed in the Ready Queue.
  2. Each process gets CPU for a fixed Time Quantum.
  3. If the process finishes → it is removed.
  4. If it doesn't finish → it is preempted and moved to the end of the queue.
  5. The next process gets the CPU.

Advantages

  • Fair: Every process gets CPU time.
  • Good response time.
  • Prevents starvation.
  • Well-suited for time-sharing systems.

Disadvantages

  • Too small time quantum → many context switches and overhead.
  • Too large time quantum → behaves similar to FCFS.
  • Average waiting/turnaround time may be higher than SJF/SRTF.

Important Interview Question

Q: What happens if the time quantum is very large?

“Round Robin approaches FCFS because each process can finish its CPU burst before the scheduler switches to another process.”

Q: What happens if the time quantum is too small?

“There will be frequent context switching, increasing overhead and reducing CPU efficiency.”

Multilevel Queue Scheduling

“Multilevel Queue Scheduling divides the ready queue into multiple separate queues based on process type or priority. Each queue can have its own scheduling algorithm, and processes are permanently assigned to a particular queue.”

How It Works

For example, queues may be:

  • System Processes
  • Interactive(Forground) Processes
  • Batch(Background) Processes

Each queue can use a different algorithm:

  • Interactive Queue → Round Robin
  • Batch Queue → FCFS

The OS also needs a method to decide which queue gets the CPU. For example, a higher-priority queue may be served before a lower-priority queue.

Key Characteristics

  • Multiple separate ready queues.
  • Each queue can have a different scheduling algorithm.
  • A process is permanently assigned to one queue.
  • Queues may have different priorities.

Advantage

“It is useful when processes can be clearly divided into different categories.”

Disadvantage

“A process in a lower-priority queue may suffer starvation if higher-priority queues continuously have processes.”

Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling (MLFQ)

Interview-ready answer:

“Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling divides the ready queue into multiple queues with different priorities and scheduling algorithms. Unlike Multilevel Queue Scheduling, a process can move between queues based on its CPU usage, priority, or behavior.”

How It Works

  • Multiple queues with different priorities.
  • Higher-priority queues usually get CPU first.
  • Each queue can use a different scheduling algorithm.
  • A process can move between queues.
  • CPU-intensive processes may move to lower-priority queues.
  • Interactive or short processes may remain in higher-priority queues.

Example

Suppose there are three queues:

Q1 → Highest Priority → Round Robin Q2 → Medium Priority → Round Robin Q3 → Lowest Priority → FCFS

A CPU-intensive process may move:

Q1 → Q2 → Q3

while an interactive process may remain in Q1.

Advantages

  • Flexible and adaptive.
  • Good for interactive systems.
  • Gives preference to short and interactive processes.
  • Can reduce starvation when aging or priority boosting is used.

Disadvantages

  • More complex to implement.
  • Requires careful selection of queue priorities and time quantum.
  • Poor configuration can cause starvation or unfairness.

MLQ vs MLFQ

MLQ → Process stays in one queue. MLFQ → Process can move between queues.

5. Process Synchronization & Concurrency Control

Process Synchronization

“Process synchronization is a mechanism used by the operating system to coordinate multiple processes or threads that access shared resources, so that they do not interfere with each other and produce incorrect results.”

Why is Synchronization Needed?

When multiple processes access shared data or resources at the same time, it can lead to a race condition and inconsistent results.

Types of Processes Based on Synchronization

There are two types of processes based on their interaction with other processes:

1. Independent Process

“An independent process does not share data or resources with other processes. Its execution does not affect or get affected by other processes.”

  • No shared data/resources.
  • Does not require process synchronization.
  • Example: Two independent programs performing unrelated calculations.

2. Cooperative Process

“A cooperative process can share data or resources with other processes, so its execution can affect or be affected by other processes.”

  • Shares data or resources.
  • Requires process synchronization.
  • Can communicate using IPC.
  • Example: Producer and Consumer processes sharing a buffer.

Race Condition

“A race condition occurs when multiple processes or threads access and modify shared data concurrently, and the final result depends on the order in which they execute.”

Critical Section

“A critical section is the part of a program where a process or thread accesses or modifies shared resources or shared data. Only one process or thread should execute its critical section at a time when mutual exclusion is required.”

Why is Critical Section Needed?

Without proper synchronization, multiple processes may access shared data simultaneously and cause a race condition.

Structure of a Critical Section

A process generally has four parts:

  1. Entry Section
    • Requests permission to enter the critical section.
    • Example: Acquiring a lock.
  2. Critical Section
    • Accesses or modifies the shared resource.
  3. Exit Section
    • Releases the lock/resource so another process can enter.
  4. Remainder Section
    • Remaining code that does not access the shared resource.

Requirements of Critical Section Solutions

A correct critical-section solution should satisfy four requirements:

  1. Mutual Exclusion
    • Only one process can be inside the critical section at a time.
    • Prevents simultaneous access to shared resources.
  2. Progress
    • If no process is in the critical section, a process that wants to enter should be allowed to proceed.
    • The decision should involve only processes that want to enter.
    • No deadlock should occur.
  3. Bounded Waiting
    • A process should not wait indefinitely.
    • There must be a limit on the number of times other processes can enter before a waiting process gets its turn.
    • Prevents starvation.
  4. No Hardware/Software Assumption
    • The solution should not depend on a particular hardware, software, or processor speed.
    • It should work independently of machine speed.

Important Points to Remember

  • Mutual Exclusion: Mandatory requirement.
  • Progress: Mandatory requirement.
  • Bounded Waiting: Not strictly mandatory, but if not satisfied, it can cause starvation.
  • No Hardware/Software Assumption: Not a mandatory condition; a solution may depend on specific hardware/software mechanisms.

Standard Synchronization Problems/Classical IPC Problems

These problems are used to understand process synchronization, mutual exclusion, deadlock, and starvation.

  1. Bounded-Buffer (Producer-Consumer) Problem
    • Producers add data to a fixed-size shared buffer, while consumers remove data.
    • Producer must not add data when the buffer is full.
    • Consumer must not remove data when the buffer is empty.
    • Requires proper synchronization to avoid race conditions.
  2. Readers-Writers Problem
    • Multiple readers can read a shared resource simultaneously.
    • Only one writer can modify the resource at a time.
    • When a writer is active, no reader or other writer can access the resource.
    • Proper priority management is needed to prevent starvation.
  3. Dining Philosophers Problem
    • Five philosophers sit around a table with five chopsticks.
    • Each philosopher needs two chopsticks to eat.
    • Demonstrates resource allocation problems.
    • Improper allocation can cause deadlock and starvation.
  4. Sleeping Barber Problem
    • A barber cuts hair when customers are present and sleeps when the shop is empty.
    • The shop has a limited number of waiting chairs.
    • If all chairs are occupied, a new customer leaves.
    • Requires synchronization between the barber and customers to avoid race conditions.

Quick Revision

Producer-Consumer → Buffer Readers-Writers → Shared resource Dining Philosophers → Chopsticks / Deadlock Sleeping Barber → Waiting chairs / Synchronization

Busy Waiting

“Busy waiting is a situation where a process continuously checks whether a condition or resource is available instead of going to sleep or blocking. It keeps using the CPU while waiting.”

Example

A process wants to enter a critical section but the lock is already held:

Check lock → Still busy → Check again → Still busy → Check again...

The process keeps checking instead of being blocked.

Why is it a Problem?

  • Wastes CPU cycles.
  • Reduces CPU efficiency.
  • Can increase power consumption.
  • Especially inefficient when the waiting time is long.

Busy Waiting vs Blocking

Busy Waiting → Process continuously checks and uses CPU. Blocking → Process sleeps and CPU is given to another process.

Thrashing

Interview-ready answer:

“Thrashing is a condition in a virtual memory system where the system spends most of its time swapping pages between main memory and disk instead of executing processes.”

Why Does Thrashing Occur?

  • Too many processes in memory.
  • Insufficient physical memory.
  • High page fault rate.
  • Processes do not have enough frames to hold their working sets.

What Happens?

More Page Faults → More Disk I/O → Less CPU Utilization → More Waiting → More Page Faults

The system becomes extremely slow.

Example

“If too many processes are running and each process needs more pages than the available RAM can hold, pages are continuously swapped in and out. The CPU spends more time handling page faults than executing processes.”

Effects

  • Very high page-fault rate.
  • Heavy disk I/O.
  • Low CPU utilization.
  • Significant performance degradation.

How to Reduce Thrashing?

  • Reduce the degree of multiprogramming.
  • Allocate more memory/frames.
  • Use working-set model.
  • Use page-fault frequency (PFF) control.

Solutions to the Critical Section Problem

Critical section solutions can be classified into four main categories:

1. Software-Based Solutions

  • Lock Variable
  • Strict Alternation (Turn Variable)
  • Peterson’s Solution
  • Dekker’s Algorithm
  • Lamport’s Bakery Algorithm

2. Hardware-Based Solutions

  • Test-and-Set Lock (TSL)
  • Compare-and-Swap (CAS)
  • Disable Interrupts

3. Operating System-Based Solutions

  • Binary Semaphore
  • Counting Semaphore

4. Compiler-Based Solutions

  • Monitors

Lock Variable

“A lock variable is a simple software-based technique used to control access to a critical section. A shared variable, usually called lock, indicates whether the critical section is free or occupied.”

How It Works

  • lock = 0 → Critical section is free.
  • lock = 1 → Critical section is occupied.
  • A process checks the lock before entering.
  • After completing the critical section, it releases the lock.

Basic Idea

Pseudocode
while (lock == 1);
lock = 1;
// Critical Section
lock = 0;

Problem with Lock Variable

Lock variable alone is not a correct solution to the critical-section problem.

The problem is that checking the lock and setting the lock are separate operations.

Example:

  • Process P1 checks lock == 0.
  • Before P1 sets lock = 1, the CPU switches to P2.
  • P2 also checks lock == 0.
  • P2 sets lock = 1 and enters the critical section.
  • P1 resumes, sets lock = 1, and also enters.

Now both processes can enter the critical section, violating mutual exclusion.

Lock Variable — Important Points

  • It uses a shared lock variable.
  • It is a busy-waiting solution because a process continuously checks the lock.
  • It can be used for more than two processes.
  • However, it does not guarantee mutual exclusion because checking and setting the lock are not atomic.
  • Therefore, lock variable is not a valid solution to the critical-section problem.
RequirementLock VariableExplanation
Mutual Exclusion❌ NoCheck and set operations are not atomic, so two processes can enter the critical section simultaneously.
Progress❌ NoDue to race conditions, a process may be delayed even when the critical section is free.
Bounded Waiting❌ NoA process may wait indefinitely, leading to starvation.
No Hardware/Software Assumption✅ YesIt does not depend on specific hardware or processor speed.

Strict Alternation (Turn Variable)

“Strict Alternation is a software-based solution for the critical-section problem that uses a shared turn variable to decide which process gets the chance to enter the critical section.”

It is designed for two processes.

How It Works

  • turn = 0 → Process P0 can enter.
  • turn = 1 → Process P1 can enter.
  • After leaving the critical section, a process gives the turn to the other process.
  • It uses busy waiting.
Pseudocode
while (turn != i);
// Critical Section
turn = j;

Example

P0 → Critical Section → P1 → Critical Section → P0 → ...

The processes must strictly take turns.

Does It Meet Critical Section Requirements?

RequirementStrict AlternationExplanation
Mutual Exclusion✅ YesOnly the process whose turn it is can enter.
Progress❌ NoA process may be forced to wait even when the other process is not interested in entering.
Bounded Waiting✅ YesA process waits for at most one turn of the other process.
No Hardware/Software Assumption✅ YesIt is a software-based solution and does not depend on hardware speed.

Main Problem

Progress violation.

Suppose P0 enters and then sets turn = 1. If P1 is doing its remainder section and does not want to enter the critical section, P0 still has to wait for P1's turn.

“Strict alternation guarantees mutual exclusion but violates progress because one process can block the other even when it does not want to enter the critical section.”

Peterson’s Solution

“Peterson’s Solution is a software-based synchronization algorithm that provides a correct solution to the critical-section problem for two processes. It uses two shared variables: flag[] and turn.”

Shared Variables

  • flag[i] → Indicates whether process Pi wants to enter the critical section.
  • turn → Indicates which process should get priority if both want to enter.

Basic Idea

Each process:

  1. Sets its flag to true to show that it wants to enter.
  2. Gives the other process the turn.
  3. Waits if the other process also wants to enter and it is the other's turn.
  4. Enters the critical section.
  5. Sets its flag to false after leaving.
Pseudocode
flag[i] = true;
turn = j;
while (flag[j] && turn == j);
// Critical Section
flag[i] = false;
// Remainder Section

Does It Meet Critical Section Requirements?

RequirementPeterson's SolutionExplanation
Mutual Exclusion✅ YesBoth processes cannot enter the critical section simultaneously.
Progress✅ YesIf the critical section is free, a process that wants to enter can proceed.
Bounded Waiting✅ YesA process cannot be postponed indefinitely.
No Hardware/Software Assumption✅ YesIt is a software-based solution and does not depend on special hardware instructions.

Important Points

  • Works for exactly two processes.
  • Uses busy waiting.
  • Provides mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.
  • Does not require special hardware instructions.
  • Mainly important for theoretical understanding; modern systems generally use hardware-supported synchronization primitives.

Dekker’s Algorithm

“Dekker’s Algorithm is a software-based solution for the critical-section problem for two processes. It uses flags and a turn variable to achieve mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.”

  • Supports 2 processes.
  • Uses busy waiting.
  • Provides mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.
  • Does not require special hardware instructions.

Interview one-liner:

“Dekker’s Algorithm uses flags and turn to safely coordinate two processes without hardware support.”

Lamport’s Bakery Algorithm

“Lamport’s Bakery Algorithm is a software-based solution that provides mutual exclusion for multiple processes using a ticket-number system, similar to customers taking tokens at a bakery.”

  • Supports multiple processes.
  • Each process takes a unique/ordered ticket number.
  • Process with the smallest ticket enters first.
  • Provides mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.
  • Uses busy waiting.

Interview one-liner:

“Lamport’s Bakery Algorithm uses ticket numbers to decide which process enters the critical section next, and it can handle multiple processes.”

Test-and-Set Lock (TSL)

“Test-and-Set is a hardware-based atomic instruction used to implement locks for mutual exclusion. It checks the current value of a lock and sets it simultaneously as one indivisible operation.”

Test-and-Set Function

Pseudocode
bool TestAndSet(bool *lock) {
    bool old = *lock;
    *lock = true;
    return old;
}

The function:

  • Returns the old value of lock.
  • Sets lock = true.
  • Both operations happen atomically.

How It Works

Pseudocode
while (TestAndSet(&lock));
// Critical Section
lock = false;
  • If lock = false → TestAndSet() returns false → process enters.
  • If lock = true → TestAndSet() returns true → process keeps waiting.
  • After leaving the critical section → lock = false.

Does It Meet Critical Section Requirements?

RequirementTSLExplanation
Mutual Exclusion✅ YesAtomic test-and-set ensures only one process acquires the lock.
Progress✅ YesIf the lock is free, a waiting process can acquire it.
Bounded Waiting❌ NoA process may repeatedly lose the lock and wait indefinitely.
No Hardware/Software Assumption❌ NoIt requires a hardware-supported atomic instruction.

Important Point

TSL uses busy waiting.

The process continuously checks the lock while waiting, so CPU cycles can be wasted. This is why it is commonly associated with a spinlock.

Compare-and-Swap (CAS)

“Compare-and-Swap is a hardware-supported atomic instruction used to implement synchronization mechanisms such as locks. It compares a memory location with an expected value and updates it only if they are equal.”

CAS Function

Pseudocode
bool CompareAndSwap(int *value, int expected, int newValue) {
    if (*value == expected) {
        *value = newValue;
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

The operation is atomic, meaning no other process can interrupt it between the comparison and update.

How It Works

Suppose:

lock = 0 → unlocked lock = 1 → locked

Pseudocode
while (!CompareAndSwap(&lock, 0, 1));
// Critical Section
lock = 0;
  • If lock == 0 → CAS changes it to 1 → process enters.
  • If lock == 1 → CAS fails → process keeps waiting.
  • After leaving → lock = 0.

Does It Meet Critical Section Requirements?

RequirementCASExplanation
Mutual Exclusion✅ YesAtomic comparison and update ensures only one process acquires the lock.
Progress✅ YesIf the lock is free, a process can acquire it.
Bounded Waiting❌ Not guaranteedBasic CAS-based locking can cause starvation.
No Hardware/Software Assumption❌ NoRequires hardware support for atomic CAS.

Important Point

CAS can be used to implement spinlocks, so a process may perform busy waiting while the lock is unavailable.

TSL vs CAS

TSL → Test old value and set lock. CAS → Compare with expected value and change to a new value only if they match.

Disable Interrupts

“Disabling interrupts is a hardware-based technique used to protect a critical section by preventing the CPU from being interrupted while the critical section is executing.”

How It Works

  1. Process enters the critical section.
  2. CPU disables interrupts.
  3. Process executes the critical section without being preempted by interrupts.
  4. Process exits the critical section.
  5. CPU enables interrupts again.
Pseudocode
DisableInterrupts();
// Critical Section
EnableInterrupts();

Does It Meet Critical Section Requirements?

RequirementDisable InterruptsExplanation
Mutual Exclusion⚠️ LimitedOn a single CPU, preventing interrupts can prevent preemption, but it is not a general solution for multiple CPUs.
Progress⚠️ LimitedCan provide progress on a single CPU, but has practical limitations.
Bounded Waiting❌ NoIt does not guarantee bounded waiting or prevent starvation.
No Hardware/Software Assumption❌ NoDirectly depends on hardware/privileged CPU support.

Important Limitations

  • Mainly applicable to single-processor systems.
  • On multiprocessor systems, disabling interrupts on one CPU does not stop another CPU from accessing the shared resource.
  • Only the kernel should normally be allowed to disable interrupts.
  • Keeping interrupts disabled for too long can affect system responsiveness.

Interview One-Liner

“Disabling interrupts can protect a critical section on a single CPU by preventing interrupt-driven preemption, but it is not suitable as a general synchronization mechanism for multiprocessor systems.”

Semaphore

“A semaphore is a synchronization mechanism used by the operating system to control access to shared resources and coordinate processes or threads.”

A semaphore is an integer variable that can only be accessed through atomic operations.

Main Operations

1. Wait / P / Down

  • Decreases the semaphore value.
  • If the resource is unavailable, the process blocks/waits.

2. Signal / V / Up

  • Increases the semaphore value.
  • Wakes up a waiting process if one exists.
Pseudocode
wait(S);
// Critical Section
signal(S);

Mutex

“A mutex (Mutual Exclusion) is a locking mechanism that allows only one thread or process at a time to access a shared resource or critical section.”

Key Points

  • Lock: Acquire mutex before entering the critical section.
  • Unlock: Release mutex after leaving.
  • Blocking: If mutex is already locked, other threads wait.
  • Ownership: Usually, the thread that locks the mutex must unlock it.
  • Prevents race conditions and protects shared data.

Mutex vs Semaphore

a mutex is a locking mechanism meant for one task at a time, while a semaphore is a signaling mechanism that manages multiple tasks at once.

FeatureMutexSemaphore
TypeObject/locking mechanismInteger-based synchronization mechanism
PurposeMutual exclusionResource management and signaling
OperationsLock / UnlockWait / Signal
AccessOnly one thread at a timeMultiple threads depending on count
OwnershipHas ownership; usually the owner unlocks itNo ownership
ValueLocked / UnlockedInteger count
TypesNo standard subtypesBinary & Counting Semaphore
ExampleProtect one shared variableManage 3 identical resources

Types of Semaphore

There are mainly two types of semaphores:

1. Binary Semaphore

  • Value can be 0 or 1.
  • Used mainly for mutual exclusion.
  • Only one process/thread can access the protected resource at a time.
  • Similar to a lock.

Example: Protecting a critical section.

2. Counting Semaphore

  • Value can be any non-negative integer.
  • Used to manage multiple instances of a resource.
  • Allows multiple processes/threads to access the resource up to the semaphore count.

Example: If there are 3 printers, initialize semaphore to 3.

Value Interpretation

“A counting semaphore is an integer-valued semaphore used to manage multiple instances of a shared resource.”

In the classic Dijkstra semaphore model, the semaphore value can be positive, zero, or negative.

  • S > 0: Number of resources currently available.
  • S = 0: No resources are available and no process is waiting.
  • S < 0: |S| represents the number of processes waiting/blocked.

Example:

If S = -3, it means 3 processes are waiting in the semaphore queue.

Wait and Signal Operations

“wait() and signal() are the two fundamental atomic operations used to operate on a semaphore.”

1. Wait() — P / Down

  • Used to acquire a resource.
  • Decreases the semaphore value.
  • If the resource is unavailable, the process blocks/waits.

Conceptually:

Pseudocode
wait(S) {
    S--;
    if (S < 0)
        block();
}

2. Signal() — V / Up

  • Used to release a resource.
  • Increases the semaphore value.
  • If processes are waiting, one of them can be woken up.

Conceptually:

Pseudocode
signal(S) {
    S++;
    if (S <= 0)
        wakeup();
}

Example

For a semaphore S = 3:

wait(S) → S = 2 → resource acquired wait(S) → S = 1 → resource acquired signal(S) → S = 2 → resource released

Important Point

Wait and Signal must be atomic operations. Otherwise, race conditions can occur while modifying the semaphore.

Monitors

“A monitor is a high-level synchronization construct that allows only one process or thread to execute inside it at a time. It provides mutual exclusion for shared data and operations.”

Key Points

  • High-level synchronization mechanism.
  • Automatically provides mutual exclusion.
  • Only one process/thread can execute inside the monitor at a time.
  • Shared data is kept inside the monitor.
  • Uses condition variables such as wait() and signal() for coordination.
  • Helps prevent race conditions.

Example

A monitor protecting a shared buffer may provide:

  • insert() → Producer adds data.
  • remove() → Consumer removes data.
  • wait() → Process waits when the buffer is full/empty.
  • signal() → Wakes a waiting process when the condition changes.

Monitor vs Semaphore

Monitor → High-level, automatic mutual exclusion.

Semaphore → Lower-level, programmer explicitly uses wait() and signal().

Priority Inversion

Priority inversion is a scheduling problem where a high-priority process is indirectly blocked by a low-priority process because the low-priority process holds a shared resource or lock required by the high-priority process.

How Priority Inversion Happens

Suppose there are three processes:

  • L → Low Priority
  • M → Medium Priority
  • H → High Priority
  1. L acquires a lock on a shared resource.
  2. H starts and needs the same resource, so H blocks and waits for L.
  3. M becomes ready and preempts L because M has higher priority than L.
  4. M continues running while L cannot release the lock.
  5. Therefore, H is indirectly delayed by M, even though H has the highest priority.

Flow:

L holds lock → H waits for L → M preempts L → H remains blocked

Why Is It a Problem?

  • High-priority processes can experience unexpected delays.
  • Can cause missed deadlines in real-time systems.
  • In severe cases, the high-priority process may be delayed indefinitely.

Solutions

Solutions to Priority Inversion

  • Priority Inheritance Protocol: The system temporarily boosts the priority of the low-priority task (L) to match the high-priority task (H) as long as L holds the needed lock. This stops medium-priority tasks (M) from interrupting L, allowing L to release the resource quickly.
  • Priority Ceiling Protocol: Every shared resource is assigned a priority ceiling equal to the highest priority task that can ever use it. Any task that locks the resource immediately gets raised to that ceiling priority level, preventing inversion altogether.

Livelock in Priority Inversion

Livelock occurs when processes are continuously changing their state or responding to each other but no process makes meaningful progress.

In the context of priority inversion, livelock can occur when scheduling or synchronization mechanisms repeatedly change priorities or cause processes to retry, preventing useful work from progressing.

Example

Suppose:

  • L → Low priority
  • M → Medium priority
  • H → High priority

If the synchronization mechanism repeatedly causes processes to change priorities, release/ reacquire locks, or retry, the processes may remain active but fail to complete their required work.

Livelock vs Deadlock

Deadlock → Processes are blocked and do nothing.

Livelock → Processes are active but make no progress.

Producer-Consumer Solution Using Semaphores

“The Producer-Consumer problem can be solved using semaphores to synchronize access to a shared bounded buffer and prevent race conditions.”

Semaphores Used

For a buffer of size N, we use three semaphores:

  • empty = N → Number of empty slots in the buffer.
  • full = 0 → Number of filled slots in the buffer.
  • mutex = 1 → Provides mutual exclusion while accessing the buffer.

Producer

Pseudocode
wait(empty);
wait(mutex);
// Add item to buffer
signal(mutex);
signal(full);
  • wait(empty) → Ensures the buffer is not full.
  • wait(mutex) → Enters the critical section.
  • Adds an item.
  • signal(mutex) → Leaves the critical section.
  • signal(full) → Increases the number of available items.

Consumer

Pseudocode
wait(full);
wait(mutex);
// Remove item from buffer
signal(mutex);
signal(empty);
  • wait(full) → Ensures the buffer is not empty.
  • wait(mutex) → Enters the critical section.
  • Removes an item.
  • signal(mutex) → Leaves the critical section.
  • signal(empty) → Increases the number of empty slots.

Important Interview Point

Why do we need three semaphores?

empty → Prevents Producer from adding to a full buffer. full → Prevents Consumer from removing from an empty buffer. mutex → Prevents Producer and Consumer from accessing the buffer simultaneously.

Readers-Writers Problem

“The Readers-Writers problem deals with synchronizing multiple processes that access a shared resource. Multiple readers can access the resource simultaneously, but a writer requires exclusive access.”

Rules

  • Multiple readers can read simultaneously.
  • Only one writer can write at a time.
  • When a writer is writing, no reader or other writer can access the resource.
  • Synchronization is required to prevent race conditions.
  • Poor scheduling can cause starvation.

Semaphores Used

Commonly, two semaphores are used:

  • mutex = 1 → Protects the readCount variable.
  • rw_mutex = 1 → Controls access to the shared resource.

readCount → Number of readers currently reading.

Reader

Pseudocode
wait(mutex);
readCount++;
if (readCount == 1)
    wait(rw_mutex);
signal(mutex);
// Reading
wait(mutex);
readCount--;
if (readCount == 0)
    signal(rw_mutex);
signal(mutex);

Writer

Pseudocode
wait(rw_mutex);
// Writing
signal(rw_mutex);

How It Works

  • The first reader locks rw_mutex, preventing writers.
  • Other readers can enter simultaneously.
  • The last reader releases rw_mutex.
  • A writer must acquire rw_mutex, so it gets exclusive access.

Important Interview Point

Readers can share the resource with other readers, but writers cannot share it with anyone.

Problem

The reader-preference solution can cause writer starvation if readers continuously arrive.

Dining Philosophers Solution Using Semaphores

“The Dining Philosophers problem demonstrates synchronization when multiple processes compete for limited shared resources. Semaphores can be used to control access to the chopsticks and prevent deadlock.”

Basic Idea

There are 5 philosophers and 5 chopsticks.

Each philosopher needs two chopsticks to eat:

  • Left chopstick
  • Right chopstick

We use:

  • chopstick[5] → Binary semaphore for each chopstick, initialized to 1.
  • mutex = 1 → Controls access to the process of picking up chopsticks.

Semaphore Setup

Pseudocode
semaphore chopstick[5] = {1, 1, 1, 1, 1};
semaphore mutex = 1;

Philosopher

Pseudocode
wait(mutex);
wait(chopstick[i]);
wait(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]);
signal(mutex);
// Eat
signal(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]);
signal(chopstick[i]);

How It Works

  1. Philosopher requests permission using wait(mutex).
  2. Picks up the left chopstick.
  3. Picks up the right chopstick.
  4. Eats.
  5. Releases both chopsticks.
  6. Other philosophers can then use them.

Why Does mutex Help?

Without mutex, all five philosophers could pick up their left chopstick simultaneously.

Then everyone waits for their right chopstick:

P0 holds left → waits for right P1 holds left → waits for right P2 holds left → waits for right P3 holds left → waits for right P4 holds left → waits for right

This creates deadlock.

By allowing only one philosopher at a time to acquire chopsticks, this particular solution prevents that circular waiting situation.

Important Point

This solution prevents deadlock, but synchronization designs should also consider starvation/ fairness.

6. Multi-Threading Models

Thread

“A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process. A process can contain multiple threads that share the same process resources but execute independently.”

Key Points

  • A thread is a lightweight unit of execution.
  • Threads belonging to the same process share:
    • Code
    • Data
    • Heap
    • Open files/resources
  • Each thread has its own:
    • Program Counter (PC)
    • Registers
    • Stack
  • Multiple threads can execute concurrently.
  • Threads are generally faster and cheaper to create and switch than processes.

Why Do We Need Threads?

Threads are needed to perform multiple tasks concurrently within the same process.

Main Reasons

  • Concurrency: Multiple tasks can progress at the same time.
  • Better CPU Utilization: While one thread waits for I/O, another can use the CPU.
  • Responsiveness: Applications remain responsive while background tasks run.
  • Resource Sharing: Threads of the same process share memory and resources.
  • Faster Communication: Threads can communicate through shared memory more easily than separate processes.
  • Lower Overhead: Creating and switching threads is generally cheaper than creating and switching processes.
  • Parallelism: On multi-core CPUs, multiple threads can execute in parallel.

Types of Threads

There are mainly two types of threads:

1. User-Level Threads

“User-level threads are managed by a user-level thread library rather than directly by the operating system kernel.”

  • Managed by user-level libraries.
  • Kernel may not know about individual threads.
  • Fast to create and switch.
  • If one thread performs a blocking system call, the entire process may block.
  • Cannot achieve true parallelism on multiple cores in many-to-one models.

Examples: POSIX Pthreads, Java threads depending on implementation.

2. Kernel-Level Threads

“Kernel-level threads are directly managed by the operating system kernel.”

  • Managed by the OS kernel.
  • Kernel schedules individual threads.
  • If one thread blocks, other threads can continue.
  • Can achieve true parallelism on multi-core CPUs.
  • Creation and context switching generally have higher overhead than user-level threads.

Process vs Thread — 5 Differences

FeatureProcessThread
1. DefinitionIndependent program in execution.Smallest unit of execution within a process.
2. MemoryHas its own separate address space.Shares memory/address space with other threads of the same process.
3. Resource SharingResources are generally independent.Shares code, data, heap, and open files with other threads.
4. Creation & SwitchingMore expensive and slower.Less expensive and faster.
5. FailureFailure of one process generally does not directly affect another process.Failure of one thread can affect the entire process.

Deadlock

A Deadlock is a situation where each of the computer process waits for a resource which is being assigned to some another process. In this situation, none of the process gets executed since the resource it needs, is held by some other process which is also waiting for some other resource to be released.

7. Deadlocks & Resource Allocation

Deadlock vs Starvation vs Livelock

FeatureDeadlockStarvationLivelock
MeaningProcesses wait for each other indefinitely.A process waits indefinitely because other processes keep getting resources/CPU.Processes remain active but make no useful progress.
Process StateUsually blocked/ waiting.Usually ready/waiting for a resource or CPU.Running/active, continuously responding or changing state.
ProgressNo progress.Other processes may make progress, but one process does not.No meaningful progress despite activity.
Main CauseCircular resource dependency.Unfair scheduling/resource allocation.Processes repeatedly react to each other.
ExampleP1 waits for P2's resource, while P2 waits for P1's resource.Low-priority process keeps waiting while higher-priority processes are repeatedly scheduled.Two processes repeatedly change/retry their actions to avoid conflict but neither completes.
SolutionPrevention, avoidance, detection & recovery.Aging, fair scheduling, bounded waiting.Better synchronization, backoff, or randomized waiting.

Easy Way to Remember

Deadlock → Stuck and waiting

Starvation → One process keeps waiting

Livelock → Active but not progressing

Necessary Conditions for Deadlock

Deadlock can occur only when all four conditions exist simultaneously:

1. Mutual Exclusion

  • A resource can be used by only one process at a time.
  • It cannot be shared simultaneously.

2. Hold and Wait

  • A process holds one or more resources while waiting for additional resources.

3. No Preemption

  • A resource cannot be forcibly taken from a process.
  • The process must release the resource voluntarily.

4. Circular Wait

  • A circular chain of processes exists.
  • Each process is waiting for a resource held by the next process.

Strategies for Handling Deadlock

There are four main strategies for handling deadlocks:

1. Deadlock Prevention

Ensure that at least one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock never occurs.
