  • Break Mutual Exclusion
  • Break Hold and Wait
  • Allow Preemption
  • Prevent Circular Wait

2. Deadlock Avoidance

The OS checks resource allocation before granting a request and ensures the system remains in a safe state.

  • Banker's Algorithm is the most common example.
  • Requires information about future resource requirements.

3. Deadlock Detection and Recovery

Allow deadlocks to occur, then detect them and recover from them.

Recovery methods:

  • Terminate processes.
  • Preempt resources.
  • Roll back processes.

4. Ignore the Deadlock

The OS simply ignores certain deadlocks if detecting and preventing them is too expensive or the deadlock is rare.

This approach is sometimes called the Ostrich Algorithm.

Easy Revision

Prevention → Make deadlock impossible

Avoidance → Stay in a safe state

Detection & Recovery → Detect and fix

Ignore → Do nothing

Deadlock Prevention

“Deadlock prevention is a technique that ensures at least one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock never occurs.”

Methods of Deadlock Prevention

1. Prevent Mutual Exclusion

  • Allow multiple processes to use a resource simultaneously (where possible) .
  • Example: Read-only files can be shared.
  • Not possible for inherently non-shareable resources like printers.

2. Prevent Hold and Wait

  • A process must request all required resources at once before execution.
  • Or, it must release currently held resources before requesting new ones.

3. Prevent No Preemption

  • Allow preemption of resources. If a process requests a resource that’s unavailable, force the process holding the requested resource to release it

4. Prevent Circular Wait

  • Assign a unique priority number to each resource, and processes must request resources in a strict priority order, preventing circular chains of waiting. o This is the most practical method to implement.

Easy Revision

Mutual Exclusion → Make resources shareable

Hold & Wait → Request all resources together

No Preemption → Take/release resources when necessary

Circular Wait → Follow resource ordering

Deadlock Detection

“Deadlock detection allows deadlocks to occur and then checks whether the system has entered a deadlocked state.”

The detection method depends on whether resources have single or multiple instances.

1. Single Instance of Each Resource

Use a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG).

A Resource Allocation Graph contains:

  • Process nodes: represented by circles.
  • Resource nodes: represented by rectangles.
  • Request edge: P → R means the process is requesting the resource.
  • Allocation edge: R → P means the resource is allocated to the process.

If every resource has only one instance:

Cycle in RAG → Deadlock

Example:

P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1

This cycle indicates deadlock.

A Wait-For Graph (WFG) can also be used by removing resource nodes:

P1 → P2 means P1 is waiting for a resource held by P2.

Cycle in WFG → Deadlock

2. Multiple Instances of Resources

A Resource Allocation Graph alone is not sufficient to determine deadlock simply by looking for a cycle, because a resource type may have multiple instances.

Use a Deadlock Detection Algorithm based on:

  • Available → Currently available resources.
  • Allocation → Resources currently allocated to each process.
  • Request → Resources currently requested by each process.

The algorithm checks whether processes can finish one by one using the available resources.

  • If all processes can finish → No deadlock.
  • If some processes cannot finish → Those processes are deadlocked.

Easy Revision

Single Instance → Resource Allocation Graph → Cycle = Deadlock

Single Instance → Wait-For Graph → Cycle = Deadlock

Multiple Instances → Detection Algorithm → Available + Allocation + Request

Deadlock Recovery

“Deadlock recovery is the process of restoring the system to a safe state after a deadlock has been detected.”

There are mainly two approaches:

1. Process Termination

Terminate one or more processes involved in the deadlock.

  • Terminate all deadlocked processes → Fast but causes more loss of work.
  • Terminate one process at a time → Continue until the deadlock is removed.

The OS may consider:

  • Process priority.
  • Resources held by the process.
  • Resources still required.
  • How much work the process has completed.

2. Resource Preemption

“Take a resource from one process and allocate it to another process to break the deadlock.”

Steps:

  1. Select a victim → Choose a process whose resource will be taken.
  2. Preempt the resource → Take the resource from that process.
  3. Rollback → Restore the affected process to a previous safe state.
  4. Restart → Continue the process later.

Problems with Recovery

  • Starvation: The same process may repeatedly be selected as the victim.
  • Data loss: Terminating or rolling back processes can cause loss of work.
  • Overhead: Recovery operations consume system resources.

Easy Revision

Deadlock Detected → Recover

Process Termination → Kill processes

Resource Preemption → Take resource + Rollback

Deadlock Avoidance

“Deadlock avoidance is a technique where the OS carefully allocates resources and ensures that the system always remains in a safe state, thereby avoiding deadlock.”

Basic Idea

Before allocating a resource, the OS checks:

“Will granting this request keep the system in a safe state?”

  • If Yes → Resource is allocated.
  • If No → Process must wait.

Safe State

A system is in a safe state if there exists at least one safe sequence in which all processes can complete their execution without causing deadlock.

Safe State ≠ Deadlock

Unsafe State ≠ Guaranteed Deadlock, but it means the system may enter deadlock.

Algorithms Used

1. Banker's Algorithm

  • Used when resources have multiple instances.
  • Checks whether allocating resources keeps the system safe.

2. Resource Allocation Graph Algorithm

  • Used for systems with single instances of each resource type.
  • Uses claim/request information to determine whether allocation can safely proceed.

Requirements

Deadlock avoidance generally requires the OS to know information such as:

  • Available resources
  • Currently allocated resources
  • Maximum resource requirements of processes

Prevention vs Avoidance

Deadlock Prevention → Break one of the four necessary conditions.

Deadlock Avoidance → Carefully allocate resources to remain in a safe state.

Banker's Algorithm

“Banker’s Algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance algorithm that checks whether granting a resource request will keep the system in a safe state.”

It is mainly used when multiple instances of resources are available.

Main Data Structures

  1. Available
    • Number of currently available instances of each resource.
  2. Max
    • Maximum resources each process may need.
  3. Allocation
    • Resources currently allocated to each process.
  4. Need
    • Remaining resources required by each process.

Formula:

Need = Max − Allocation

Basic Steps

  1. Calculate the Need matrix.
  2. Find a process whose: Need ≤ Available
  3. Assume that process completes.
  4. Add its allocated resources back: Available = Available + Allocation
  5. Repeat for all processes.
  6. If all processes can finish → Safe State.
  7. If no suitable process can be found → Unsafe State.

Example Idea

Suppose:

Available = 3

Process P1 needs 2 resources.

Since:

Need(P1) ≤ Available

P1 can finish.

After P1 finishes, its allocated resources are released and added to Available. Then another process may become able to finish.

This creates a Safe Sequence.

Safe Sequence

A sequence such as:

P1 → P3 → P4 → P0 → P2

means processes can complete in this order without causing deadlock.

Important Point

Safe State → At least one safe sequence exists.

Unsafe State → No safe sequence can be found; deadlock is possible.

8. Main Memory Management & Allocation Strategies

Memory Management

Memory Management is an important function of the operating system that manages main memory (RAM) and controls how memory is allocated and used by processes.

The OS is responsible for:

  • Allocating memory to processes.
  • Deallocating memory when a process finishes.
  • Keeping track of which memory areas are free and occupied.
  • Protecting one process's memory from another.
  • Supporting virtual memory when RAM is insufficient.
  • Efficiently using available memory.

Goal: - Efficient utilization of memory by minimizing the internal and external fragmentation.

Introduction to Memory

Memory is a storage area used by the computer to store data and instructions that are currently being used by the CPU.

The CPU directly works with data and instructions present in main memory (RAM).

A simple flow is:

Secondary Storage → RAM → CPU

Memory Units

Memory is measured using different units:

  • 1 Bit = Smallest unit of memory, either 0 or 1.
  • 1 Byte (B) = 8 bits.
  • 1 KB = 1024 Bytes.
  • 1 MB = 1024 KB.
  • 1 GB = 1024 MB.
  • 1 TB = 1024 GB.
  • 1 PB = 1024 TB.

Memory Cell: Smallest storage unit that holds 1 bit of data. Each address in memory typically refers to a byte.

Word & Byte: A word is a group of bits; 1 byte = 8 bits.

Capacity: Total number of bits a memory can hold.

Formula to Find Memory Capacity

The basic formula is:

Memory Capacity = Number of Memory Locations × Bits per Location

Classification of Memory

Computer memory is broadly classified into Primary Memory and Secondary Memory.

1. Primary Memory

Primary memory is memory that the CPU can directly access.

  • Faster than secondary memory.
  • Limited capacity.
  • Used to store programs and data currently being processed.
  • Includes RAM and ROM.

RAM — Random Access Memory

RAM is the main working memory of a computer that temporarily stores programs and data currently being used by the CPU.

  • Volatile → Data is lost when power is turned off.
  • Fast access.
  • Supports multitasking.

Types of RAM

SRAM — Static RAM

  • Faster and more expensive.
  • Does not require periodic refreshing.
  • Commonly used for CPU cache.

DRAM — Dynamic RAM

  • Slower and cheaper than SRAM.
  • Requires periodic refreshing.
  • Commonly used as main memory (RAM).
  • Includes SDRAM and DDR variants.

ROM — Read-Only Memory

ROM is non-volatile memory that stores instructions required for system startup and firmware.

  • Data is retained even when power is off.
  • Commonly stores firmware and boot instructions.

Types of ROM

  • MROM: Programmed during manufacturing.
  • PROM: Can be programmed once.
  • EPROM: Can be erased using ultraviolet (UV) light and reprogrammed.
  • EEPROM: Can be electrically erased and reprogrammed.
  • Flash Memory: Electrically erasable/reprogrammable memory widely used in storage devices.

2. Secondary Memory

Secondary memory is used for long-term storage of data and programs.

  • Non-volatile.
  • Larger capacity.
  • Slower than primary memory.
  • CPU does not normally access it directly; data is loaded into RAM before execution.

Examples:

  • HDD
  • SSD
  • USB drives
  • Memory cards
  • Optical discs
  • Magnetic tapes

Easy Revision

Primary Memory → CPU-accessible → Faster → RAM + ROM

Secondary Memory → Long-term storage → Slower + Larger → HDD + SSD + USB etc.

Loading

Loading is the process of transferring an executable program from secondary storage into main memory (RAM) so that the CPU can execute it.

The loader performs this task.

Types of Loading

1. Static Loading

  • Entire program is loaded into memory before execution.
  • Program remains in memory during execution.
  • Memory requirement is determined beforehand.
  • No code/data is loaded on demand.

2. Dynamic Loading

  • Only the required part of the program is loaded initially.
  • Other parts are loaded on demand during execution.
  • Saves memory because unused parts need not be loaded.

Static Loading → Load everything initially

Dynamic Loading → Load when needed

Linking

Linking is the process of combining object files and required libraries to create an executable file.

Static Linking

  • Libraries are included in the executable before execution.
  • Executable size is larger.
  • No need to load those libraries separately at runtime.

Dynamic Linking

  • Libraries are linked/loaded at runtime.
  • Executable contains references to shared libraries.
  • Examples: .so in Linux and .dll in Windows.
  • Reduces executable size and allows libraries to be shared.

Static Linking → Library included in executable

Dynamic Linking → Library loaded when required

Address Binding

Address binding is the process of mapping a program's logical addresses to actual physical memory addresses.

There are three types:

1. Compile-Time Binding

  • Starting memory location is known at compile time.
  • Compiler generates absolute addresses.
  • If the starting address changes, the program must be recompiled.

Known at compile time → Absolute address

2. Load-Time Binding

  • Memory location is not known at compile time.
  • Compiler generates relocatable code.
  • Loader adjusts addresses when loading the program into memory.

Binding happens when program is loaded

3. Execution-Time / Dynamic Binding

  • Address mapping is performed during execution.
  • Process can be moved from one memory location to another.
  • Requires hardware support such as the MMU (Memory Management Unit).

Binding happens during execution → MMU required

Techniques in Memory Allocation

Memory allocation is the process of assigning available memory space to processes when they need it.

There are two major techniques:

1. Contiguous Memory Allocation

A process is allocated one continuous block of physical memory.

Types:

  • Fixed Partitioning
  • Variable/Dynamic Partitioning

Advantages:

  • Simple to implement.
  • Fast memory access.

Disadvantages:

  • Can cause internal or external fragmentation.
  • Difficult to utilize memory efficiently.

2. Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation

A process can be divided into multiple parts and stored in different locations in memory.

Types:

  • Paging
  • Segmentation
  • Segmentation with Paging

Advantages:

  • Better memory utilization.
  • Reduces external fragmentation.
  • Supports virtual memory.

Disadvantages:

  • More complex memory management.
  • Requires additional data structures such as page tables or segment tables.

Fixed Partitioning

Fixed Partitioning is a contiguous memory allocation technique in which main memory is divided into a fixed number of partitions of fixed sizes before or during system operation.

Each partition can hold at most one process.

How It Works

Suppose RAM is divided into 4 partitions:

100 MB | 200 MB | 300 MB | 400 MB

If a process requires 150 MB:

  • It can be placed in the 200 MB partition.
  • The remaining 50 MB inside that partition cannot be used by another process.

Types

1. Equal-Sized Partitions

  • All partitions have the same size.
  • Simple to implement.
  • Can waste more memory for small processes.

2. Unequal-Sized Partitions

  • Partitions have different sizes.
  • A process can be placed in a suitably sized partition.
  • Provides better memory utilization than equal-sized partitions.

Advantages

  • Simple and easy to implement.
  • Low management overhead.
  • Fast allocation and deallocation.

Disadvantages of Fixed Partitioning

  1. Internal Fragmentation Unused space inside an allocated partition is wasted. Example: 4 MB partition − 3 MB process = 1 MB wasted.
  2. External Fragmentation Free space exists but is divided into separate non-contiguous blocks, so it cannot be used for a larger process.
  3. Process Size Limitation A process larger than the largest partition cannot be loaded.
  4. Low Degree of Multiprogramming Maximum number of processes is limited by the number of partitions.

Variable / Dynamic Partitioning

Variable partitioning is a contiguous memory allocation technique where partitions are created dynamically according to the size of the process.

  • Partition size is not fixed.
  • A process gets memory approximately equal to its requirement.
  • Better memory utilization than fixed partitioning.
  • Causes external fragmentation.
  • Does not usually cause internal fragmentation.

Example:

Process = 10 MB → Allocate 10 MB

Process = 25 MB → Allocate 25 MB

Advantages

  • Better memory utilization.
  • No fixed partition size.
  • Process size is not limited by predefined partitions.

Disadvantages of Variable Partitioning

1. External Fragmentation

  • Free memory becomes divided into small, non-contiguous blocks.
  • A process may not fit even if the total free memory is sufficient.
  • Example: Two free blocks of 1 MB + 1 MB cannot hold a 2 MB process because they are not contiguous.

2. Complex Memory Allocation

  • Partition sizes change dynamically.
  • OS must continuously track allocated and free memory blocks.
  • Allocation and deallocation are more complex.

Compaction

Compaction combines scattered free memory into one large contiguous block by moving processes.

Purpose: Reduce external fragmentation.

Disadvantage:

  • Computationally expensive.
  • Moving large amounts of memory takes significant time.
  • Processes may need to be temporarily paused during relocation.

Swapping

Swapping is a memory management technique in which a process is temporarily moved between main memory (RAM) and secondary storage to free RAM for other processes.

How It Works

  • Swap Out: Process is moved from RAM → secondary storage.
  • Swap In: Process is brought back from secondary storage → RAM.
  • The process can continue execution after being swapped back in.

Advantages

  • Allows more processes to be handled with limited RAM.
  • Improves degree of multiprogramming.
  • Higher-priority processes can be brought into memory when needed.

Disadvantage

  • Swapping is slow because secondary storage is much slower than RAM.
  • Transfer time depends on the amount of data being moved.

Partition Allocation Policies

Partition allocation policies decide which free memory block should be allocated to a process in variable/dynamic partitioning.

1. First Fit

  • Start searching from the beginning of memory.
  • Allocate the first block large enough for the process.
  • Fast and simple.

First suitable block → Allocate

2. Best Fit

  • Search all available blocks.
  • Allocate the smallest block that is large enough.
  • Can create many small free holes.

Smallest suitable block → Allocate

3. Worst Fit

  • Search all available blocks.
  • Allocate the largest available block.
  • Leaves a relatively large remaining block.

Largest block → Allocate

4. Next Fit

  • Similar to First Fit.
  • Starts searching from the position of the last allocation, not from the beginning.
  • Wraps around to the beginning if necessary.

Start from last position → First suitable block

Quick Comparison

PolicySelectsSearch Starts
First FitFirst suitable blockBeginning
Best FitSmallest suitable blockBeginning
Worst FitLargest blockBeginning
Next FitFirst suitable blockLast allocation position

Easy Trick

First Fit → First

Best Fit → Smallest

Worst Fit → Largest

Next Fit → Next from last position

Buddy System

Buddy System is a memory allocation technique that divides memory into blocks of power-of-two sizes and efficiently splits and merges them during allocation and deallocation.

How It Works

Allocation:

Find the smallest power-of-2 block that can satisfy the request.

If the block is too large, repeatedly split it into two equal-sized buddies.

Allocate one buddy and keep the other free.

Deallocation:

Free the allocated block.

Check whether its buddy is also free.

If yes → merge (coalesce) them.

Continue merging upward if possible.

Example

Request = 18 KB

128 KB
↓
64 KB + 64 KB
↓
32 KB + 32 KB

Since 16 KB < 18 KB, allocate 32 KB.

18 KB request → 32 KB allocated → 14 KB internal fragmentation

Key Properties

Blocks are usually powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...

Fast allocation and deallocation

Fast splitting and merging

Reduces external fragmentation

Can cause internal fragmentation

Advantages

Fast allocation/deallocation

Easy coalescing of free blocks

Simple memory management

Reduces external fragmentation

Disadvantages

Internal fragmentation due to power-of-two allocation

Requested size may be much smaller than allocated block

Some memory is wasted

Logical and Physical Address

Logical Address

Logical address is the address generated by the CPU for a process during execution.

  • Also called a virtual address.
  • The process uses logical addresses.
  • It does not directly represent the actual location in RAM.
  • The MMU (Memory Management Unit) translates it into a physical address.

Physical Address

Physical address is the actual address in main memory (RAM) where the data or instruction is stored.

  • Generated after address translation.
  • Used by the memory hardware to access RAM.
  • Different processes can have the same logical address but different physical addresses.

Address Translation

CPU → Logical Address → MMU → Physical Address → RAM

Example:

CPU generates logical address 1000

MMU translates it to physical address 5000

RAM accesses location 5000

Memory Management Unit (MMU)

MMU is a hardware component that translates logical (virtual) addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses in main memory (RAM).

How MMU Works

CPU → Logical Address → MMU → Physical Address → RAM

Example:

CPU generates Logical Address = 1000

MMU translates it to Physical Address = 5000

RAM accesses location 5000

Main Functions

  • Address Translation: Converts logical address → physical address.
  • Memory Protection: Prevents one process from accessing another process's memory.
  • Relocation: Allows a process to be loaded at different physical memory locations.
  • Supports Virtual Memory: Helps map virtual addresses to physical memory using techniques such as paging and segmentation.

Important Point

The CPU generates the logical address, while the MMU performs the address translation.

Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation

Non-contiguous allocation is a memory allocation technique where a process is divided into multiple parts and these parts can be stored at different locations in physical memory.

The process does not need one continuous block of memory.

Types

  1. Paging
    • Process is divided into fixed-size pages.
    • Physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames.
    • Pages can be placed in any available frames.
    • Eliminates external fragmentation.
  2. Segmentation
    • Process is divided into logical segments such as code, data, and stack.
    • Segments can have different sizes.
    • Can cause external fragmentation.
  3. Segmentation with Paging
    • Combines segmentation and paging.
    • Each segment is further divided into pages.

Advantages

  • Better memory utilization.
  • Process does not require contiguous memory.
  • Supports virtual memory.
  • Paging eliminates external fragmentation.

Disadvantages

  • More complex than contiguous allocation.
  • Requires additional structures such as page tables/segment tables.
  • Address translation adds overhead.

Paging

  • Paging is a non-contiguous memory management technique in which a process is divided into fixed-size blocks called pages, while physical memory is divided into equal-size blocks called frames.
  • Page size = Frame size
  • Pages of a process can be stored in any available frames.
  • A process does not need contiguous physical memory.
  • Only required pages may be loaded into RAM, supporting virtual memory.

Why Do We Need Paging?

Without paging, a process needs a contiguous block of memory, which can cause external fragmentation.

Paging solves this by:

  • Allowing pages to be placed anywhere in RAM.
  • Eliminating external fragmentation.
  • Supporting execution of programs larger than available physical memory through virtual memory.
  • Making memory allocation easier using fixed-size pages and frames.
  • Logical Address Space or Virtual Address Space: The Logical Address Space, refers to the set of all possible logical addresses that a process can generate during its execution.
  • Physical Address Space: The Physical Address Space refers to the total range of addresses available in a computer's physical memory (RAM).

Page Table

A data structure maintained by the OS that maps page numbers to frame numbers.

Basic Paging Structure

Logical Address = [ Page Number | Page Offset ]
Page Table:
Page Number → Frame Number
Physical Address = [ Frame Number | Frame Offset ]

Since page size and frame size are equal:

Page Offset = Frame Offset

Logical Address

A logical address is divided into:

Logical Address = Page Number + Page Offset

Where:

  • p = Page number
  • d = Page offset

Physical Address

A physical address is divided into:

Physical Address = Frame Number + Frame Offset

Where:

  • f = Frame number
  • d = Frame offset

Address Translation

Suppose the CPU generates:

Logical Address = (Page Number, Offset)

The MMU:

  1. Extracts the page number.
  2. Uses the page number to access the page table.
  3. Finds the corresponding frame number.
  4. Combines the frame number with the same offset.
  5. Generates the physical address.

Page Number → Page Table → Frame Number

Page Table Base Register — PTBR

PTBR (Page Table Base Register) contains the physical address of the first entry/start of the page table.

When a process is switched:

  • OS loads the corresponding page table address into the PTBR.
  • MMU uses PTBR to locate the page table.

Important:

PTBR stores the address of the page table, not the page number.

Effective Access Time with and without PTBR

PTBR (Page Table Base Register) stores the starting physical address of the page table.

Without PTBR

If the page table is stored in main memory, but there is no PTBR, the system needs an extra mechanism/register to locate the page table. Conceptually, the access still requires:

  1. Access page table.
  2. Access actual data/instruction.

If main memory access time = m:

EAT = m + m = 2m

With PTBR

PTBR directly contains the base address of the page table.

However, PTBR does not eliminate the page-table memory access.

For every memory reference:

  1. PTBR gives the location of the page table.
  2. Access page table → m
  3. Access actual data → m

Therefore:

EAT = 2m

Paging with TLB

TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is a small, fast cache that stores recently used page number → frame number mappings.

It reduces the time required to access the page table in main memory.

Working

CPU generates:

Logical Address = Page Number + Offset

Then:

  1. CPU sends the page number to TLB.
  2. TLB Hit: Page number is found → frame number is obtained directly.
  3. TLB Miss: Page number is not found → page table in main memory is accessed.
  4. Frame number + offset gives the physical address.
  5. Actual data is accessed from RAM.

TLB Hit

CPU → TLB → Physical Memory

If:

  • TLB lookup = t
  • Memory access = m

Then:

Time = t + m

TLB Miss

CPU → TLB → Page Table → Physical Memory

Time:

Time = t + m + m

Time = t + 2m

Effective Access Time (EAT)

If:

  • α = TLB hit ratio
  • t = TLB lookup time
  • m = main memory access time

Then:

EAT = α(t + m) + (1 − α)(t + 2m)

Simplified:

EAT = t + m + (1 − α)m

Important Interview Point

PTBR is used to locate the page table; it is not a cache.

TLB is what reduces the extra page-table lookup.

Page Table Entry (PTE)

Page Table Entry (PTE) is an entry in the page table that stores information needed to map a virtual page/logical page to a physical frame and control access to that page.

Information Stored in PTE

1. Frame Number

  • Identifies the physical frame where the page is stored.
  • Frame number bits:

Frame Number Bits = log₂(Physical Memory / Frame Size)

2. Present / Absent Bit

  • Tells whether the page is currently in RAM.
  • 1 → Page is present
  • 0 → Page is absent → Page Fault

3. Protection Bits

  • Specify allowed operations:
    • R → Read
    • W → Write
    • X → Execute
  • Prevent unauthorized memory access.

4. Referenced / Accessed Bit

  • Set when the page is accessed.
  • Used by page replacement algorithms such as LRU/Clock.

5. Cache Bit

  • Determines whether caching is enabled for the page.
  • Useful for memory-mapped I/O, where fresh values may be required.

6. Dirty / Modified Bit

  • Indicates whether the page has been modified after being loaded into RAM.
  • Dirty = 1: Page must generally be written back before replacement.
  • Dirty = 0: Page can generally be discarded without writing it back.

Basic Paging Structure

Logical Address = [ Page Number | Page Offset ]
Page Table:
Page Number → Frame Number
Physical Address = [ Frame Number | Frame Offset ]

Since:

Page Size = Frame Size

Therefore:

Page Offset = Frame Offset

Important Address Terms

Logical Address (LA)

Number of bits required to represent one logical address.

Physical Address (PA)

Number of bits required to represent one physical address.

Logical Address Space (LAS)

Total size of the logical/virtual address space of a process, measured in bytes.

LAS = 2^LA bytes

Physical Address Space (PAS)

Total size of the physical memory, measured in bytes.

PAS = 2^PA bytes

LA vs LAS

TermMeaningUnit
LABits required to represent one logical addressBits
LASTotal logical address spaceBytes

LAS = 2^LA

Example:

LA = 32 bits

LAS = 2³² bytes = 4 GB

PA vs PAS

TermMeaningUnit
PABits required to represent one physical addressBits
PASTotal physical address spaceBytes

PAS = 2^PA

Example:

PA = 32 bits

PAS = 2³² bytes = 4 GB

Number of Pages

If:

  • LAS = Logical Address Space
  • PS = Page Size
  • p = Page number bits

Then:

Number of Pages = LAS / PS

Since:

LAS = 2^LA

and

PS = 2^d

Therefore:

Number of Pages = 2^(LA − d)

Hence:

p = LA − d

or:

2^p = LAS / PS

Number of Frames

If:

  • PAS = Physical Address Space
  • FS = Frame Size
  • f = Frame number bits

Then:

Number of Frames = PAS / FS

Since:

PAS = 2^PA

and:

FS = PS = 2^d

Therefore:

Number of Frames = 2^(PA − d)

Hence:

f = PA − d

or:

2^f = PAS / FS

Address Format

Logical address:

LA = p + d

where:

  • p = Page number bits
  • d = Page offset bits

Physical address:

PA = f + d

where:

  • f = Frame number bits
  • d = Frame offset bits

Therefore:

Page Offset Bits = Frame Offset Bits

Number of Entries in Page Table

Each process has one page table.

Number of PTEs = Number of Pages

Therefore:

Number of PTEs = 2^p

Page Table Entry Size

A PTE must contain the frame number.

Therefore:

PTE Size = Number of bits required to represent a frame

PTE Size = f bits

But remember: if the question asks for PTE size in bytes, convert:

PTE Size = f / 8 bytes

Page Table Size

Page Table Size = Number of Pages × PTE Size

If PTE is given in bits:

PT Size = 2^p × f bits

If PTE is given in bytes:

PT Size = 2^p × PTE Size bytes

Average Internal Fragmentation

For fixed-size pages:

Average Internal Fragmentation ≈ Page Size / 2

More precisely, assuming random process size:

Average Internal Fragmentation = (Page Size − 1) / 2

For large page sizes, this is approximately:

Average Internal Fragmentation ≈ 50% of Page Size

Example:

Page Size = 4 KB

Average Internal Fragmentation ≈ 2 KB

TLB Access Time

Let:

  • t = TLB lookup time
  • m = main memory access time
  • α = TLB hit ratio

TLB Hit:

Time = t + m

TLB Miss:

Time = t + 2m

Effective Access Time:

EAT = α(t + m) + (1 − α)(t + 2m)

Simplified:

EAT = t + m + (1 − α)m

Without TLB

Page table is in main memory.

EAT = 2m

Because:

  1. Access page table.
  2. Access actual data/instruction.

Multilevel Paging

If the page table itself becomes too large, we divide it into multiple levels.

First calculate:

Entries per Page = Page Size / PTE Size

If:

  • Page Size = 2^d
  • PTE Size = 2^e

Then:

Entries per Page = 2^(d−e)

Therefore:

Bits represented by each level = log₂(Entries per Page)

Bits per Level = d − e

Finding Number of Levels

First calculate:

Page Number Bits = LA − Page Offset Bits

Then:

Number of Levels = ⌈Page Number Bits / Bits per Level⌉

Therefore:

Number of Levels = ⌈(LA − d) / log₂(Page Size / PTE Size)⌉

Finding Outer Page Table

Suppose the first-level page table requires:

2^m pages

Then the outer page table needs:

2^m entries

Therefore:

Outer Page Table Size = 2^m × PTE Size

If PTE size is f bits:

Outer PT Size = 2^m × f bits

To find how many pages are required for the outer page table:

Pages Required = Outer PT Size / Page Size

Quick Multilevel Paging Shortcut

Use this order:

1. Find Offset Bits

2. Find Page Number Bits

3. Find Entries Per Page

4. Find Bits Per Level

5. Divide Page Number Bits by Bits Per Level

6. Ceiling → Number of Levels

Formula:

Offset = log₂(Page Size)

Page Bits = LA − Offset

Entries/Page = Page Size / PTE Size

Bits/Level = log₂(Entries/Page)

Levels = ⌈Page Bits / Bits/Level⌉

EAT for Multilevel Paging

If there are n levels of page tables and each memory access takes m:

EAT = (n + 1)m

Because:

  • n memory accesses → page-table levels
  • 1 memory access → actual data

Example:

2-level paging:

EAT = (2 + 1)m = 3m

3-level paging:

EAT = (3 + 1)m = 4m

With a TLB, a TLB hit can avoid the page-table walks, while a TLB miss requires the page-table levels to be accessed.

Multilevel Paging

Multilevel paging is a technique in which the page table itself is divided into multiple levels, so that the entire page table does not need to be stored as one large contiguous block.

Why Do We Need Multilevel Paging?

In a simple paging system, every process needs a page table.

For a large process, the page table can become very large.

Example:

  • Process Size = 16 MB = 2²⁴ bytes
  • Page Size = 1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes
  • PTE Size = 4 bytes

Step 1: Number of Pages

Number of Pages = Process Size / Page Size

= 2²⁴ / 2¹⁰

= 2¹⁴ = 16,384 pages

Therefore, the page table needs 16,384 PTEs.

Step 2: Size of Page Table

Page Table Size = Number of Pages × PTE Size

= 16,384 × 4

= 65,536 bytes = 64 KB

So, the page table itself is 64 KB.

Now page table size > frame size so how we can store this in main memory so we need to divided page table into multiple pages

Multilevel paging solves this problem by paging the page table itself.

How Multilevel Paging Works

Instead of:

One large page table

we create:

Outer Page Table → Inner Page Tables → Frames

The outer page table contains pointers to inner page tables.

Only the required inner page tables need to be created.

Step 3: Entries Per Page

Each page/frame is 1 KB = 1024 bytes.

Each PTE = 4 bytes.

Therefore:

Entries per Page = Page Size / PTE Size

= 1024 / 4

= 256 = 2⁸ entries

So, one page can hold 256 PTEs.

Step 4: Number of Inner Page Tables

Total PTEs:

16,384 = 2¹⁴

Each inner page table can contain:

256 = 2⁸ PTEs

Therefore:

Number of Inner Page Tables = 2¹⁴ / 2⁸

= 2⁶ = 64

So we need 64 inner page tables.

Each inner page table occupies 1 KB.

Step 5: Outer Page Table

The outer page table needs 64 entries, one for each inner page table.

Each entry is 4 bytes:

Outer Page Table Size = 64 × 4

= 256 bytes

Since:

256 bytes < 1 KB

the outer page table fits inside one page/frame.

Segmentation

Segmentation is a memory management technique in which a process is divided into variable-sized units called segments, where each segment represents a logical part of a program such as functions, arrays, or modules.

It follows the user’s logical view of memory

segmentation divides a process based on its logical structure, not into equal-sized blocks.

Why Do We Need Segmentation?

Paging divides a process into fixed-size pages, but it does not represent the logical structure of a program.

Segments can have different lengths, depending on the program’s requirements.

Segments represent meaningful units like code, stack, data, or modules

Logical Address in Segmentation

A logical address is divided into:

Logical Address = Segment Number + Offset

For example:

(Segment 2, Offset 500)

means:

Go to Segment 2 and access the location 500 bytes from its beginning.

Segment Table

The OS maintains a Segment Table.

Each segment-table entry typically contains:

  • Base → Starting physical address of the segment.
  • Limit → Size/length of the segment.
  • Protection bits → Read/Write/Execute permissions.

Address Translation

CPU generates:

Segment Number + Offset

The MMU:

  1. Uses the segment number to access the segment table.
  2. Gets Base and Limit.
  3. Checks:

Offset < Limit

  1. If valid:

Physical Address = Base + Offset

  1. If Offset ≥ Limit:

Segmentation Fault

Advantages

Represents the logical structure of a program.

Easy to provide different protection levels to different segments.

Segments can grow independently.

Supports sharing of logical program components.

Disadvantages

Segments are variable-sized, causing external fragmentation.

Memory allocation is more complex.

May require compaction.

Segmentation vs Paging

FeaturePagingSegmentation
DivisionFixed-size pagesVariable-size segments
Based onPhysical memory managementLogical program structure
AddressPage + OffsetSegment + Offset
FragmentationInternalExternal
ExamplePage 5Code segment
Programmer viewUsually invisibleLogical structure is visible

Why Segmentation Instead of Only Paging?

Paging focuses on efficient physical memory allocation, while segmentation focuses on the logical organization and protection of a program.

Segmentation with Paging

Segmentation with paging is a memory management technique that combines both segmentation and paging to overcome their individual limitations.

It solves some limitations of using only segmentation or only paging.

Why Do We Need Segmentation with Paging?

Problem with Segmentation:

  • Segments are variable-sized.
  • Can cause external fragmentation.
  • Large segments can be difficult to allocate contiguously.

Problem with Paging:

  • Pages are fixed-sized.
  • Paging does not naturally represent the logical structure of a program.

Therefore:

Segmentation → Logical View

Paging → Efficient Physical Memory Allocation

Basic Structure

A process is divided into segments.

Each segment is further divided into pages.

Physical memory is divided into frames.

Process
├── Segment 0
│   ├── Page 0
│   └── Page 1
├── Segment 1
│   ├── Page 0
│   └── Page 1
└── Segment 2
    ├── Page 0
    └── Page 1

Pages map to physical frames.

Logical Address

The logical address is divided into:

[ Segment Number | Page Number | Page Offset ]

Where:

  • Segment Number (s) → identifies the segment.
  • Page Number (p) → identifies the page within that segment.
  • Offset (d) → identifies the exact location within the page.

Address Translation

CPU generates:

Segment Number + Page Number + Offset

Then:

Step 1: Segment number is used to access the segment table.

Step 2: Segment table gives the address of the page table for that segment.

Step 3: Page number is used to access that page table.

Step 4: Page table gives the frame number.

Step 5: Frame number + offset gives the physical address.

CPU
↓
Segment Number
↓
Segment Table
↓
Page Table
↓
Frame Number
↓
Physical Memory

Important Formula

If:

  • Page size = 2ᵈ bytes

Then:

Offset bits = d

If logical address size = m bits:

Segment Bits + Page Number Bits + Offset Bits = m

Overlays in Memory Management

Overlay is a memory-management technique where only the required part of a program is loaded into main memory, while other parts remain on secondary storage and are loaded when needed.

It was mainly used when physical memory was smaller than the size of the complete program.

Why Do We Need Overlays?

Suppose:

Program size = 20 MB

Available RAM = 10 MB

The entire program cannot fit into RAM.

With overlays, the program is divided into modules:

Main program
├── Module A
├── Module B
└── Module C

Only the modules required at a particular time are loaded into RAM.

For example:

RAM
┌──────────────┐
│ Main program │
│ Module A     │
└──────────────┘

Later:

RAM
┌──────────────┐
│ Main program │
│ Module B     │
└──────────────┘

Module A can be replaced by Module B because they are not needed simultaneously.

How Overlays Work

  1. Divide the program into smaller modules.
  2. Identify modules that are not required simultaneously.
  3. Keep only the required modules in RAM.
  4. When another module is required, load it into the overlay area.
  5. The new module replaces the previous module.

Virtual Memory

9. Virtual Memory, Demand Paging & Page Replacement

Virtual Memory is a memory-management technique that allows a process to execute even when the entire process is not loaded into physical RAM.

It uses secondary storage (disk/SSD) as an extension of RAM and loads required parts of a process into memory on demand.

Why Do We Need Virtual Memory?

Suppose:

Process size = 10 GB

Available RAM = 4 GB

Normally, the entire process cannot fit into RAM.

With virtual memory:

Only the required pages are loaded into RAM.

The remaining pages stay on disk until they are needed.

Virtual Memory vs Overlay

Both allow a program larger than RAM to execute, but the major difference is who manages what gets loaded into memory.

FeatureOverlayVirtual Memory
Managed byProgrammerOS + Hardware
LoadingProgrammer explicitly loads modulesOS automatically loads pages
UnitModules/parts of programPages (or segments)
Address translationNot necessarily requiredRequired
Page faultNoYes
Memory protectionLimitedSupported
Programmer involvementHighVery low
Modern systemsRare/mostly obsoleteWidely used

How Virtual Memory Works

  1. CPU generates a virtual/logical address.
  2. MMU translates it using the page table.
  3. If the required page is in RAM:
    • Access continues normally.
    • This is a page hit.
  4. If the page is not in RAM:
    • A page fault occurs.
  5. OS loads the required page from disk into a free frame.
  6. Page table is updated.
  7. The interrupted instruction is restarted.

Page Fault

Occurs when the required page is not present in RAM.

Demand Paging

Pages are loaded into RAM only when they are actually needed.

Swap Space

Disk/SSD area used to temporarily store memory pages that are not currently in RAM.

Virtual Memory vs Physical Memory

Virtual MemoryPhysical Memory
Logical/virtual address spaceActual RAM
LargerLimited
Managed by OS + MMUActual hardware memory
Uses pagesUses frames
Can use disk as backing storeFaster than disk

Types of Virtual Memory

Virtual memory can be implemented mainly using:

  1. Paging
  2. Segmentation

The MMU (Memory Management Unit) translates virtual addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses.

1. Paging

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into equal-size frames.

Only required pages are loaded into RAM. Pages not currently in memory remain in secondary storage.

Virtual Memory
Pages
↓
Page Table
↓
Physical Memory
Frames

Key points:

  • Page = fixed-size block of virtual memory.
  • Frame = fixed-size block of physical memory.
  • Page Size = Frame Size
  • Page table maps Page → Frame.
  • If required page is not in RAM → Page Fault.
  • OS loads the page from secondary storage into RAM.

Page Fault Service Time

Page Fault Service Time (s) = total time required to handle a page fault and make the required page available in RAM.

If:

  • m = normal memory access time
  • s = page fault service time
  • p = page fault rate

Then:

EAT = (1 − p)m + ps

or

EAT = m + p(s − m)

Important: This simplified formula assumes s already includes the required page-fault handling and memory access overhead.

2. Segmentation

Segmentation divides virtual memory into variable-sized logical segments.

Examples:

  • Code
  • Data
  • Stack
  • Heap

Each segment can be loaded into memory when required.

Virtual Memory
↓
+---------+
| Code |
| Data |
| Stack |
| Heap |
+---------+
↓
Segment Table
↓
Physical Memory

Key points:

  • Segments are variable-sized.
  • Segment table stores information such as:
    • Base address
    • Limit
    • Protection
    • Present/valid information
  • Required segments can be brought into memory when needed.

Demand Paging

Demand Paging is a virtual-memory technique in which a page is loaded into RAM only when it is actually required by the CPU.

Unlike loading the complete process into memory, demand paging loads pages on demand.

Pure Demand Paging

Pure Demand Paging means a process starts execution with none of its pages loaded into RAM.

The first time a page is referenced:

Page Fault → OS loads the page → Execution continues

After some pages have been loaded, subsequent references to those pages can execute without a page fault.

Key point:

Pure demand paging may cause many page faults when a process starts because initially no pages are in memory.

Working Process of Demand Paging

CPU generates a virtual address
└── Check the page table
    ├── Page present → Access RAM
    └── Page absent → Page fault
        ├── Invalid reference → Raise an exception
        └── Valid reference
            1. Obtain a frame, replacing a page if necessary.
            2. Load the required page.
            3. Update the page table.
            4. Restart the instruction.

Steps

  1. CPU references a page.
  2. MMU checks the page table.
  3. Present bit = 1 → page is already in RAM.
  4. Present bit = 0 → page fault occurs.
  5. OS checks whether the memory reference is valid.
  6. OS finds a free frame.
  7. Required page is loaded from secondary storage.
  8. Page table is updated.
  9. Present bit is set to 1.

10. Faulting instruction is restarted.

What Happens If No Free Frame Exists?

If RAM has no free frame:

Page Replacement Algorithm is used.

The OS selects a victim page and replaces it with the required page.

Common algorithms:

  • FIFO
  • LRU
  • LFU
  • MRU
  • Random

How Demand Paging Affects Performance

Demand paging improves memory utilization, but page faults are expensive.

Normal memory access:

RAM → Fast

Page fault:

RAM → Disk/SSD → RAM → Continue execution

Therefore:

Page fault time ≫ Memory access time

Even a small page-fault rate can significantly increase the effective access time.

Effective Access Time

If:

  • m = normal memory access time
  • s = page-fault service time
  • p = page-fault rate

Then:

EAT = (1 − p)m + ps

or:

EAT = m + p(s − m)

If p increases significantly:

EAT increases → System performance decreases

Factors Affecting Demand Paging Performance

  • Page fault rate
  • Page fault service time
  • Memory access time
  • Page replacement algorithm
  • Number of available frames
  • Disk/SSD speed
  • Locality of reference

Demand Paging vs Pre-Paging

FeatureDemand PagingPre-Paging
LoadingLoads page when neededLoads pages before they are needed
Main ideaJust in timeLoad in advance
Initial page faultsMore likelyCan reduce them
Memory usageGenerally lowerCan be higher
RiskMore page faultsMay load unnecessary pages
Best whenAccess pattern is unpredictablePages have strong locality

Page Fault

A page fault occurs when a process references a virtual page that is not currently available in the required physical memory location.

It is a trap to the operating system, which then decides how to handle the reference.

Causes of Page Fault

1. Demand Paging

  • Required page is not currently in RAM.
  • OS loads it from secondary storage.

2. Invalid Memory Access

  • Process accesses an address outside its valid address space.
  • Example: accessing memory that was never allocated.

3. Protection Violation

  • Process accesses a page in an unauthorized way.
  • Example: trying to write to a read-only page.

Types of Page Fault

1. Minor Page Fault

Required data is already available in physical memory, so no disk I/O is required.

Example: The page may already be in RAM but needs to be mapped into the process's address space.

2. Major Page Fault

Required page is not in RAM and must be fetched from secondary storage.

This is expensive because it involves I/O.

3. Invalid Page Fault

Process makes an invalid memory reference or violates memory protection.

The OS generally terminates the process or raises an appropriate exception.

Steps in Page Fault Handling

  1. CPU generates a virtual address.
  2. MMU checks the page table.
  3. Present bit = 0 → page fault occurs.
  4. Control transfers to the OS.
  5. OS checks whether the memory reference is valid.
  6. If invalid → process gets an exception/termination.
  7. If valid → OS finds a free frame.
  8. If no free frame exists → page replacement is performed.
  9. Required page is read from secondary storage.

10. Page table is updated.

11. Present bit is set.

12. Faulting instruction is restarted.

Impact on Performance

Page faults are expensive because:

Disk/SSD access ≫ RAM access

Frequent page faults can cause:

Increased Latency

  • Processes spend more time waiting for I/O.

Reduced CPU Utilization

  • CPU may remain idle while waiting for page I/O.

Thrashing

  • Excessive page faults cause the system to spend more time swapping/pages handling than executing processes.

Important Interview Point

Not every page fault requires disk access.

  • Minor fault → usually no disk I/O.
  • Major fault → disk/secondary-storage I/O required.
  • Invalid fault → invalid/protected memory access.

Swap Space

Swap space is a portion of secondary storage (usually disk/SSD) used by the operating system to temporarily store pages or memory contents that are not currently needed in RAM.

It acts as a backing store for virtual memory.

Why Do We Need Swap Space?

RAM is limited.

When RAM becomes heavily occupied, the OS can move less-used pages from RAM to swap space:

RAM → Swap Space

When the page is needed again:

Swap Space → RAM

This frees RAM for other processes.

Swap Out

Moving a page/process from RAM to secondary storage.

RAM → Disk

Swap In

Bringing a page/process back from secondary storage into RAM.

Disk → RAM

Swap Space and Page Fault

Suppose a page was previously moved to swap:

  1. Process references the page.
  2. Page is not present in RAM.
  3. Page fault occurs.
  4. OS finds the page in swap space.
  5. Page is loaded into a physical frame.
  6. Page table is updated.
  7. Instruction is restarted.

Swap Space vs Page File

Conceptually they serve the same purpose, but terminology differs by OS:

  • Linux/Unix: Usually called swap space and can be a swap partition or swap file.
  • Windows: Uses a page file.

Page Replacement Algorithms

Page replacement is required when a page fault occurs and there is no free frame in RAM.

The OS must choose a victim page to remove and replace it with the required page.

Page Replacement Steps

  1. Page fault occurs.
  2. Check for a free frame.
  3. If no free frame exists, select a victim page.
  4. If victim page is dirty, write it back to disk.
  5. Load the required page into the freed frame.
  6. Update the page table.
  7. Restart the interrupted instruction.

Common Algorithms

  1. FIFO — First In First Out
  2. Optimal
  3. LRU — Least Recently Used
  4. MRU — Most Recently Used

1. FIFO

Replace the page that entered memory first.

Think of it as a queue:

First In → First Out

Advantages:

  • Very simple.
  • Easy to implement using a queue.

Disadvantage:

  • May remove an important frequently used page.
  • Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly.

2. Optimal Page Replacement

Replace the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.

Advantages:

  • Produces the minimum possible number of page faults.
  • Used as a benchmark for other algorithms.

Disadvantage:

  • Cannot be implemented practically because the OS does not know future page references.

Optimal = Best theoretical algorithm

3. LRU

Replace the page that has not been used for the longest time in the past.

Advantages:

  • Generally performs well.
  • Based on locality of reference.
  • Does not suffer from Belady's Anomaly.

Disadvantage:

  • Tracking exact usage history can be expensive.

LRU = Look backward

4. MRU

Replace the page that was used most recently.

Disadvantage:

  • Usually performs worse than LRU for typical workloads.
  • Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly.

MRU = Remove the most recently used page

Quick Comparison

AlgorithmVictim PageFuture KnowledgeBelady's Anomaly
FIFOOldest pageNoYes
OptimalUsed farthest in futureYesNo
LRULeast recently usedNoNo
MRUMost recently usedNoCan occur

Belady's Anomaly

Belady's Anomaly is a phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames causes the number of page faults to increase instead of decrease.

Normally:

More Frames → Fewer Page Faults

But during Belady's Anomaly:

More Frames → More Page Faults

Why Does It Happen?

It occurs in some non-stack page replacement algorithms, where increasing the number of frames can change the replacement order in an unfavorable way.

The most famous example is:

FIFO

Belady's Anomaly in FIFO

Reference String:

1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5

Using FIFO:

FramesPage Faults
39
410

So:

3 frames → 9 faults

4 frames → 10 faults

Even though we increased the number of frames, page faults increased.

This is Belady's Anomaly.

Stack Property

A stack algorithm has the property that:

Pages present with N frames are always a subset of pages present with N+1 frames.

Therefore:

Increasing frames cannot increase page faults.

Examples:

  • LRU
  • Optimal

These do not suffer from Belady's Anomaly.

Why FIFO Suffers

FIFO only considers:

When was the page loaded?

It does not consider whether the page is frequently used.

Therefore, increasing the number of frames can change the FIFO replacement order and cause a useful page to be removed.

Algorithms and Belady's Anomaly

AlgorithmBelady's Anomaly
FIFOYes
OptimalNo
LRUNo
Second ChanceCan occur
RandomCan occur
LFUDepends on implementation; not generally guaranteed to be anomaly-free

Important Correction

Do not memorize:

“LFU is always a stack algorithm.”

The safe interview answer is:

“Stack algorithms such as LRU and Optimal do not suffer from Belady's Anomaly.”

Thrashing

Thrashing occurs when the OS spends more time handling page faults and swapping pages between RAM and disk than executing processes.

Cycle of Thrashing:

  • High multiprogramming: Too many processes are loaded into memory.
  • Insufficient frames: Each process receives fewer memory frames than required.
  • Frequent page replacement: More page faults lead to continuous swapping between memory and disk.

This repeated cycle of low CPU utilization -> more processes -> more page faults is called Thrashing.

Role of Locality of Reference

Locality of reference means a process tends to access a small group of pages repeatedly during a period of time.

This group is called the working locality.

How to Control Thrashing

  1. Reduce degree of multiprogramming
  2. Allocate more frames
  3. Use Working Set Model
  4. Use Page Fault Frequency
  5. Suspend some processes if necessary

Working Set Model

The Working Set Model keeps enough pages in memory to support the process's current locality.

Let:

  • WSSᵢ = Working Set Size of process i
  • Δ = Working-set window
  • D = Total memory demand
  • m = Total available frames

Formula:

D = Σ WSSᵢ

If:

D > m → Thrashing

If:

D ≤ m → No thrashing

Example:

P1 WSS = 4 frames

P2 WSS = 5 frames

P3 WSS = 3 frames

D = 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 frames

If available frames:

m = 10

Then:

D > m → Thrashing

Page Fault Frequency (PFF)

PFF controls thrashing by monitoring the page-fault rate.

Page-fault rate
├── Above upper limit → Allocate more frames
├── Within limits     → Keep the current allocation
└── Below lower limit → Reclaim some frames
  • Fault rate > upper limit → Allocate more frames.
  • Fault rate < lower limit → Remove/reallocate some frames.
  • No available frames → Suspend a process and give its frames to others.

Memory Interleaving

Memory interleaving is a technique that divides main memory into multiple independent banks so that consecutive memory accesses can be handled in parallel or overlapped, increasing memory bandwidth.

Why Is It Needed?

A single memory bank can become a bottleneck because the CPU may have to wait for one memory operation to finish.

With multiple banks:

Multiple memory operations can be overlapped → Higher memory performance

How It Works

Suppose memory has 4 banks:

Address 0 → Bank 0
Address 1 → Bank 1
Address 2 → Bank 2
Address 3 → Bank 3
Address 4 → Bank 0
Address 5 → Bank 1
...

So consecutive addresses are distributed across different banks.

Types

1. Low-Order Interleaving

Lower-order address bits select the memory bank.

Address → Bank
0 → 0
1 → 1
2 → 2
3 → 3
4 → 0
  • Consecutive addresses go to different banks.
  • Good for sequential memory access.

2. High-Order Interleaving

Higher-order address bits select the memory bank.

Large contiguous block → Bank 0
Next block → Bank 1
Next block → Bank 2
  • Consecutive addresses within a block remain in the same bank.
  • Useful when accesses are localized within blocks.

Quick Comparison

FeatureLow-OrderHigh-Order
Bank selectionLower address bitsHigher address bits
Consecutive addressesDifferent banksUsually same bank
Good forSequential accessBlock/localized access

Key Point

Memory interleaving improves memory throughput, not necessarily the latency of a single memory access.

10. File Systems & Storage Organization

File System in Operating System

A file system is a method used by the OS to organize, store, name, access, and manage files and directories on storage devices.

Why Do We Need a File System?

  • Organize files and directories.
  • Provide easy file access.
  • Manage storage space.
  • Track file locations.
  • Provide file protection and permissions.
  • Support file creation, deletion, reading, and writing.

Basic File System Structure

User
↓
Application
↓
File System
↓
Storage Management
↓
Disk / SSD

File

A file is a named collection of related data stored on secondary storage.

Common file types:

  • Text files
  • Executable files
  • Images
  • Videos
  • Documents

Directory

A directory is a data structure used to organize and locate files.

Example:

/home/dilip/
├── resume.pdf
├── notes.txt
└── projects/
    ├── app.cpp
    └── README.md

Main Functions of File System

  1. File Creation
  2. File Deletion
  3. Read / Write
  4. File Naming
  5. Directory Management
  6. Space Management
  7. File Protection
  8. File Access Control

File Attributes

A file generally has:

  • Name
  • Type
  • Size
  • Location
  • Owner
  • Permissions
  • Creation/modification time

File Operations

Common operations:

Create

Open

Read

Write

Seek

Close

Delete

File System Examples

File SystemCommon Usage
FAT32USB drives, older systems
NTFSWindows
ext4Linux
APFSmacOS
XFSLinux/servers

Important Interview Point

File System ≠ Storage Device

A storage device provides physical storage, while the file system determines how the OS organizes and accesses data on that storage.

Linux File System

Linux uses a hierarchical file system where everything starts from the root directory /.

Linux File System Structure

/
├── bin → Essential user commands
├── boot → Bootloader and kernel files
├── dev → Device files
├── etc → System configuration files
├── home → User home directories
├── lib → Essential shared libraries
├── media → Mounted removable devices
├── mnt → Temporary mount point
├── opt → Optional software
├── proc → Process and kernel information
├── root → Home directory of root user
├── run → Runtime information
├── sbin → System administration commands
├── tmp → Temporary files
├── usr → User applications and utilities
└── var → Logs, cache, variable data

Important Directories

DirectoryPurpose
/Root of entire file system
/homeUser files
/rootRoot user's home
/etcConfiguration files
/binEssential commands
/sbinSystem commands
/devDevice files
/procProcess/kernel information
/tmpTemporary files
/varLogs and changing data
/bootBoot-related files
/usrApplications and utilities

Key Linux Concept

“Everything is a file”

Linux represents many resources as files, including:

  • Regular files
  • Directories
  • Devices
  • Pipes
  • Sockets

For example:

/dev/sda

represents a storage device.

File System Hierarchy

Linux follows a tree-like hierarchical structure:

/
├── home/
│   └── dilip/
│       └── notes.txt
├── etc/
│   └── config
└── var/
    └── log/

Every file has a unique path.

Example:

/home/dilip/notes.txt

Common Linux File Systems

  • ext4 → Most commonly used Linux file system
  • XFS → High-performance/server workloads
  • Btrfs → Copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums
  • ext3/ext2 → Older Linux file systems

Inode

An inode stores metadata about a file, but normally does not store the file name or file data itself.

It contains information such as:

  • File type
  • File permissions
  • Owner
  • File size
  • Timestamps
  • Links
  • Pointers to data blocks

Think:

File name → inode → data blocks

Path Name in File Directory

A path name is the location of a file or directory in the file system. It tells the OS how to reach that file from a particular starting point.

Types of Path Names

1. Absolute Path

Starts from the root directory / and gives the complete path.

Example:

/home/dilip/projects/app.cpp

  • Always starts with /.
  • Does not depend on the current directory.
  • Uniquely identifies the location.

2. Relative Path

Specifies the location relative to the current working directory.

Suppose current directory is:

/home/dilip/projects

Then:

./app.cpp

or

../notes.txt

  • . → Current directory
  • .. → Parent directory

Absolute vs Relative Path

FeatureAbsolute PathRelative Path
Starts fromRoot /Current directory
Depends on current directoryNoYes
Example/home/dilip/a.txt../a.txt
LengthUsually longerUsually shorter

Path Example

/home/dilip/projects/app.cpp

/                   Root directory
└── home/           Home directories
    └── dilip/      User's home directory
        └── projects/
            └── app.cpp  File

Special Path Symbols

SymbolMeaning
/Root directory
.Current directory
..Parent directory
~Current user's home directory

Structures of Directory in Operating System

Directory structure defines how files and directories are organized and accessed by the operating system.

1. Single-Level Directory

All files are stored in one directory.

Directory
├── file1.txt
├── file2.txt
└── file3.txt

Advantages:

  • Very simple.
  • Easy to implement.

Disadvantages:

  • File-name conflicts.
  • Difficult to organize many files.
  • Not suitable for multiple users.

2. Two-Level Directory

Each user gets a separate directory.

Master directory
├── User 1/
│   ├── a.txt
│   └── b.txt
└── User 2/
    ├── a.txt
    └── b.txt

Advantages:

  • Different users can have files with the same name.
  • Better isolation between users.

Disadvantages:

  • Limited directory organization.
  • Difficult to share files between users.

3. Tree-Structured Directory

Directories can contain subdirectories, forming a tree.

/
├── home
│ └── dilip
    │ ├── notes
    │ └── projects
        │ └── app.cpp
├── etc
└── var

Advantages:

  • Easy organization.
  • Supports hierarchical directories.
  • Efficient file searching.
  • Most modern OSes use this structure.

Disadvantage:

  • Sharing files between directories can be more complicated.

4. Acyclic Graph Directory

Allows sharing of files or directories, but does not allow cycles.

In the earlier directory structures, a file could only be accessed from the directory it was stored in. The acyclic graph directory structure solves this by allowing a file or subdirectory to be shared across multiple directories using links. Changes made by one user are visible to all users sharing that file.

/home/user1/shared.txt ──┐
                        ├──→ Same shared file
/home/user2/shared.txt ──┘

The same file can be accessed from multiple directories using links.

Advantages:

  • Supports file/directory sharing.
  • Avoids duplicate copies.

Disadvantages:

  • More complex than a tree.
  • Need to manage links carefully.

5. General Graph Directory

Allows directories to contain links that can create cycles.

A ──→ B ──→ C
↑           │
└───────────┘

Here, a cycle can exist.

Advantages:

  • Very flexible.
  • Supports extensive sharing.

Disadvantages:

  • Searching can get stuck in cycles.
  • Garbage collection may be required.
  • More complex to manage.

Quick Comparison

StructureMain IdeaSharingCycle
Single-LevelOne directoryNoNo
Two-LevelOne directory per userLimitedNo
TreeHierarchicalLimitedNo
Acyclic GraphSharing using linksYesNo
General GraphArbitrary linksYesPossible

Easy Way to Remember

Single → One directory

Two-Level → One per user

Tree → Hierarchy

Acyclic Graph → Sharing, no cycle

General Graph → Sharing + cycles

File Allocation Methods

File allocation methods determine how the blocks of a file are stored on secondary storage.

The main methods are:

  1. Contiguous Allocation
  2. Linked Allocation
  3. Indexed Allocation

1. Contiguous Allocation

File blocks are stored in consecutive disk blocks.

File A → [10][11][12][13][14]

Advantages:

  • Very fast sequential access.
  • Very fast random access.
  • Simple implementation.

Disadvantages:

  • External fragmentation.
  • Difficult to grow a file.
  • May require compaction.

Example:

If a file needs 5 blocks and starts at block 10:

Blocks = 10, 11, 12, 13, 14

2. Linked Allocation

File blocks can be stored anywhere on the disk, with each block pointing to the next block.

[7] → [19] → [4] → [25] → NULL

Advantages:

  • No external fragmentation.
  • Files can easily grow.
  • Any free block can be used.

Disadvantages:

  • Poor random access.
  • Pointer requires extra space.
  • If a pointer is corrupted, part of the file may become inaccessible.

Best for: Sequential access.

3. Indexed Allocation

A separate index block stores pointers to all data blocks of the file.

Index block
├── Entry 0 → Data block 7
├── Entry 1 → Data block 19
├── Entry 2 → Data block 4
└── Entry 3 → Data block 25

The index block contains addresses of the file's data blocks.

Advantages:

  • Supports direct/random access.
  • No external fragmentation.
  • Files can grow easily.

Disadvantages:

  • Extra space required for index block.
  • Large files may require multiple index blocks.

Quick Comparison

FeatureContiguousLinkedIndexed
StorageConsecutiveAnywhereAnywhere
Random AccessFastSlowFast
Sequential AccessFastFastFast
External FragmentationYesNoNo
File GrowthDifficultEasyEasy
Extra Pointer SpaceNoYesYes
Main ProblemFragmentationRandom accessIndex overhead

Easy Way to Remember

Contiguous → Together

Linked → Chain

Indexed → Index points to blocks

File Access Methods in Operating System

File access methods define how a process reads and accesses data stored in a file.

The main access methods are:

  1. Sequential Access
  2. Direct (Random) Access
  3. Indexed Access

1. Sequential Access

Data is accessed in order, from beginning to end.

Block 1 → Block 2 → Block 3 → Block 4

To access Block 4, the system normally passes through the previous blocks.

Example:

  • Reading a text file line by line.
  • Playing an audio/video stream.

Advantages:

  • Simple.
  • Efficient for sequential processing.

Disadvantage:

  • Slow when you need data in the middle/end directly.

Think: Tape

2. Direct / Random Access

Any block can be accessed directly without reading previous blocks.

        ┌── Block 1
        ├── Block 2
Request ─┼── Block 5 ← Directly access
        └── Block 8

Example:

  • Database files.
  • Disk-based applications.

Advantages:

  • Fast access to a specific location.
  • Suitable for large files.

Disadvantage:

  • Requires support for locating the required block.

Think: Array

3. Indexed Access

An index stores pointers to the locations of records/blocks, allowing fast searching and access.

Index
├── Entry A → Block 2
├── Entry B → Block 7
└── Entry C → Block 15

The system first searches the index and then accesses the required block.

Advantages:

  • Fast searching.
  • Supports both sequential and direct access.
  • Useful for large files and databases.

Disadvantage:

  • Extra memory/storage is required for the index.

Quick Comparison

FeatureSequentialDirect / RandomIndexed
Access orderIn sequenceAny locationThrough index
Random accessNoYesYes
Speed for specific recordSlowFastFast
Extra index requiredNoNoYes
ExampleLog/text fileDatabase fileIndexed database

Access Method vs Allocation Method

Don't confuse these two:

File Allocation → Where are file blocks stored?

Contiguous, Linked, Indexed

File Access → How do we access those blocks?

Sequential, Direct, Indexed

11. Secondary Storage, Disk Structure & Disk Scheduling

Secondary Memory

Secondary memory is non-volatile storage used to store data and programs permanently. It has larger capacity but is slower than primary memory.

Types of Secondary Memory

1. Fixed Devices

Storage devices that are normally installed inside the computer and are not frequently removed.

Examples:

  • HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
  • SSD (Solid State Drive)
  • Internal NVMe SSD

Features:

  • Large storage capacity
  • Non-volatile
  • Used for OS, applications, and user data
  • Usually faster than removable storage

2. Removable Devices

Storage devices that can be easily connected and removed from a computer.

Examples:

  • USB Flash Drive
  • Memory Card (SD/microSD)
  • External HDD/SSD
  • CD/DVD

Features:

  • Portable
  • Easy data transfer
  • Can be used across multiple computers
  • Usually connected through USB or other removable interfaces

HDD vs SSD

HDD (Hard Disk Drive) uses magnetic rotating disks, while SSD (Solid State Drive) uses flash memory and has no moving parts.

FeatureHDDSSD
TechnologyMagnetic diskFlash memory
Moving partsYesNo
SpeedSlowerFaster
Boot timeHigherLower
LatencyHigherLower
NoiseYesSilent
Power consumptionHigherLower
DurabilityLowerHigher
Cost/GBCheaperMore expensive
CapacityUsually larger/cheaperUsually smaller for same budget
Shock resistanceLowerHigher

HDD Working

CPU
↓
Disk Controller
↓
Spindle → Rotating Platter
↓
Read/Write Head
↓
Data

Data is stored magnetically on rotating platters.

SSD Working

CPU
↓
SSD Controller
↓
Flash Memory Cells
↓
Data

Data is stored electronically in NAND flash memory cells.

Interview One-Liner

“HDD stores data magnetically on rotating platters, making it cheaper but slower, while SSD uses NAND flash with no moving parts, making it much faster, more durable, and energy-efficient.”

Disk Structure

Disk structure describes how data is physically organized and accessed on a storage disk, especially an HDD.

HDD Structure

An HDD consists mainly of:

  • Platters → Circular disks where data is stored.
  • Tracks → Concentric circles on a platter.
  • Sectors → Small divisions of a track that store data.
  • Read/Write Head → Reads or writes data.
  • Spindle → Rotates the platters.
  • Cylinder → Set of tracks at the same radius across all platters.
Platter (schematic)
┌─────────────────────────┐
│  ┌───────────────────┐  │
│  │ Track             │  │
│  │ ┌───────┬───────┐ │  │
│  │ │Sector │Sector │ │  │
│  │ └───────┴───────┘ │  │
│  └───────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────┘
             ↑
          Spindle

Important Terms

1. Platter

Circular magnetic disk used to store data.

2. Track

A circular path on the platter.

Track 0

Track 1

Track 2

Track 3

3. Sector

A track is divided into smaller units called sectors.

Traditionally:

1 sector = 512 bytes

Modern disks may also use:

4 KB sectors

4. Cylinder

A cylinder is a collection of tracks at the same position/radius on all platters.

Platter 1 → Track 5
Platter 2 → Track 5
Platter 3 → Track 5
↓
Cylinder 5

5. Read/Write Head

Moves over the platter to read or write data.

Disk Access Time

Total time required to access data from a disk starting from initial request to the completion of data transfer,

Access time = Seek time + Rotational latency + Transfer time + Overhead

Seek Time:

Time required to move the read/write head to move to track where the required data is located.

Total seekTime=No of seeks * seek time

Rotational Latency:

Time waiting for the required sector to rotate under the head.

Average rotational latency:

Average rotational latency = 1/2 × rotation time

If disk speed is RPM:

Rotation time = 60 / RPM seconds

Therefore:

Average rotational latency = 30 / RPM seconds

Transfer Time:

Time required to read/write data from disk once the read/write head is position over the correct track and correct sector.

Data transfer time = data size/transfer rate

Transfer rate = no of bytes transfer per unit time or speed at which data is transferred.

Disk Capacity Formula

For a disk:

Disk Capacity = Number of Platters × Number of Surfaces/Platter × Tracks/Surface × Sectors/Track × Bytes/Sector

But if formatting overhead is given, you need to subtract the space reserved for metadata/control information.

With Formatting Overhead

If formatting overhead is given as a percentage:

Usable Capacity = Raw Capacity × (1 − Overhead/100)

Example:

Raw capacity = 1 TB
Formatting overhead = 5%

Usable capacity = 1 TB × (1 − 5/100) = 0.95 TB

If Overhead Is Given in Bytes

If the question says X bytes of overhead per sector:

Usable Bytes/Sector = Sector Size − Overhead

So:

Usable Capacity = Platters × Surfaces × Tracks × Sectors/Track × (Sector Size − Overhead)

Example:

Sector size = 512 bytes
Overhead = 12 bytes

Usable data per sector = 512 − 12 = 500 bytes

Therefore:

Usable Capacity = Total Number of Sectors × 500 bytes

Important Interview/Exam Trick

There are two different cases:

Overhead GivenFormula
PercentageRaw Capacity × (1 − overhead%)
Bytes/sectorTotal Sectors × (Sector Size − overhead)
Total bytesRaw Capacity − overhead

Remember: If overhead is specified per sector, subtract it from the sector size before multiplying by the number of sectors.

Disk Scheduling Algorithms

Disk scheduling determines the order in which pending disk I/O requests are served to minimize head movement and improve performance.

Goals

  • Minimize seek time
  • Minimize head movement
  • Reduce response time
  • Maximize throughput
  • Provide fairness
  • Avoid starvation

1. FCFS — First Come First Serve

Services requests in the order they arrive.

50 → 82 → 170 → 43 → 140 → 24 → 16 → 190

Pros: Simple, fair, no starvation Cons: High seek time, poor performance

Remember: FCFS = Arrival order

2. SSTF — Shortest Seek Time First

Always services the request closest to the current head position.

Pros: Lower average seek time, better throughput Cons: Can cause starvation of distant requests

Remember: SSTF = Nearest request first

3. SCAN — Elevator Algorithm

Head moves in one direction, services requests, reaches the disk end, then reverses.

Start at 50, moving toward higher track numbers.

50 → 82 → 140 → 170 → 190 → Disk end
Disk end → 43 → 24 → 16 (reverse direction)

Pros: Good throughput, more predictable than SSTF Cons: Unnecessary movement to disk end

Remember: SCAN = Go to end + Reverse

4. C-SCAN — Circular SCAN

Head moves in one direction only. After reaching the end, it returns to the beginning and continues.

Service requests       0 → ··· → Disk end
Return without service Disk end → 0
Resume servicing       0 → ··· → Disk end

Pros: More uniform waiting time Cons: Extra movement while returning to beginning

Remember: C-SCAN = One direction + Circular return

5. LOOK

Similar to SCAN, but the head goes only up to the last pending request, not the physical disk end.

Start at 50, moving toward higher track numbers.

50 → 82 → 140 → 170 → 190 (last request in that direction)
190 → 43 → 24 → 16 (reverse direction)

Pros: Less unnecessary movement than SCAN Cons: Waiting time can still vary

Remember: LOOK = SCAN without going to disk end

6. C-LOOK

Similar to C-SCAN, but instead of going to the physical ends, it goes only to the last request, then jumps to the request at the other end.

Pros: Less movement than C-SCAN Cons: Extra circular jump; requests may wait for a cycle

Remember: C-LOOK = C-SCAN without going to disk ends

SCAN vs LOOK

SCANLOOK
Goes to disk endGoes to last request
More head movementLess head movement
May move unnecessarilyMore efficient

C-SCAN vs C-LOOK

C-SCANC-LOOK
Goes to physical disk endGoes only to last request
Returns to beginningJumps to other end request
More movementLess movement

7. N-STEP SCAN

Divides requests into groups of N and processes one group completely before processing the next.

Main purpose: Prevent request starvation and improve fairness.

Remember: N-STEP = Divide into batches

8. F-SCAN

Uses two queues. While one queue is being serviced, new requests go into the second queue.

Queue 1 → SCAN → Complete
↓
Queue 2 → New requests

Main purpose: Prevent arm stickiness and provide fairness.

9. LIFO

Services the most recently arrived request first.

Advantage: May improve locality in some cases. Disadvantage: Old requests can suffer starvation.

10. RSS — Random Scheduling

Selects requests randomly.

Mainly useful for simulation/analysis, not practical disk scheduling.

Quick Revision Table

AlgorithmBasic IdeaStarvation
FCFSArrival orderNo
SSTFNearest requestPossible
SCANEnd → ReverseNo
C-SCANOne direction → ReturnNo
LOOKSCAN without disk endNo
C-LOOKC-SCAN without disk endsNo
N-STEP SCANProcess batchesNo
F-SCANTwo queues + SCANNo
LIFONewest firstPossible
RSSRandomUnpredictable

Most Important for Interviews

Focus mainly on:

↓

↓

↓

Easy Memory Trick

SCAN → End + Reverse

LOOK → Last Request + Reverse

Disk Interleaving

Disk interleaving is a technique of arranging sectors on a disk so that the CPU/controller gets enough time to process one sector before the next required sector arrives under the read/write head.

Why Is It Needed?

In older/slower disk systems, after reading one sector, the controller may not be ready to read the immediately next physical sector.

Without interleaving:

Sector 1 → read
↓
Controller not ready
↓
Sector 2 already passed
↓
Wait for another rotation

Interleaving places other sectors between consecutive logical sectors.

Example

Without Interleaving:

Physical: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Logical: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

With 2:1 Interleaving:

Physical: 1 5 2 6 3 7 4 8
Logical: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

After reading sector 1, the controller gets time while sectors 5 passes, then sector 2 arrives.

Types

1. 1:1 Interleaving

Logical: 1 2 3 4 5 6
Physical: 1 2 3 4 5 6

No sectors are skipped.

2. 2:1 Interleaving

One useful sector is followed by one intervening sector.

1 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 3 → 7 → 4 → 8

Key Point

Interleaving does NOT change the logical sector order. It changes their physical arrangement on the track.

Spooling in Operating System

12. I/O Systems, Spooling & Buffering

Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online) is a technique where data for a slow peripheral device is temporarily stored in a disk/queue so that multiple processes can share the device efficiently.

Why Do We Need Spooling?

Some I/O devices are slow and can handle only one operation at a time.

Example: Printer

Instead of making every process wait for the printer:

Process 1 ─┐
Process 2 ─┼──→ Spool Queue → Printer
Process 3 ─┘

Processes put their print jobs into the spool queue, and the printer processes them one by one.

Example

Suppose 3 processes want to print:

P1 → Job A ─┐
P2 → Job B ─┼→ Disk/Spool Queue → Printer
P3 → Job C ─┘

The processes can continue execution while the printer handles the jobs.

Key Points

  • Uses disk as temporary storage.
  • Useful for slow and shared devices.
  • Allows multiple processes to submit jobs.
  • Provides queuing of I/O requests.
  • Improves CPU/device utilization.

Common Example

Print Spooling

Print jobs are stored in a queue on disk and sent to the printer one by one.

Spooling vs Buffering

Both temporarily store data, but their purpose and storage mechanism are different.

FeatureSpoolingBuffering
PurposeManage a shared slow deviceHandle speed mismatch between components
StorageUsually diskUsually RAM/main memory
Multiple jobsYesUsually data stream
Device examplePrinterKeyboard, network, disk I/O
Main conceptQueueTemporary data storage
Allows process to continueYesYes, depending on operation

Easy Example

Spooling:

P1 ─┐
P2 ─┼→ Disk Queue → Printer
P3 ─┘

Buffering:

Fast Producer → RAM Buffer → Slow Consumer

Easy Difference to Remember

Spooling = Multiple jobs waiting for one shared device

Buffering = Temporary storage to handle different speeds
